Former minister arrested in Paraguay’s latest Ueno Bank failure fallout

A former economy minister has been detained, accused of financial crimes linked to Paraguay’s collapsed Ueno Bank.

Paraguay’s former economy minister Carlos Fernandez Valdovinos has turned himself in to police.

On Friday, he became the latest former official placed under arrest following the collapse of one of the country’s largest banks.

The Ueno Bank crisis, which saw millions locked out of their life savings earlier this month, has already prompted the impeachment of President Santiago Pena, who has been arrested along with several other former top officials.

An arrest warrant for Valdovinos, seen by the AFP news agency, accused the 61-year-old of “alleged criminal acts of administration for personal gain, aggravated passive bribery, criminal association and money laundering”.

The public prosecutor’s office alleged that while he was minister in July last year, he approved the transfer of tens of millions of dollars in pension fund money to Ueno Bank.

He left office in August, after which he signed a multi-million-dollar consulting contract with the business group that controlled Ueno Bank.

Prosecutors believe the lucrative contract may have been linked to the pension fund transaction.

The Ueno Bank crisis

The crisis erupted on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.

In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million customers. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions. It left people struggling to access their savings, wages and pension payments, and raised questions about the government’s handling of public money.

The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.

His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings. He was removed from office on November 6.

The bank had grown quickly under Pena’s presidency from a financial technology company into a large firm handling state pensions and the accounts of several government entities.

Pena is accused of using his position to direct millions in government funds to Ueno and concealing or downplaying its financial troubles, despite warnings of risky lending practices, while having financial ties to the bank. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares last year.

UK pensions department confirms cyberattack

November 28, 2026

The UK has confirmed a cyberattack on its welfare and pension systems, forcing several online services offline. Payments continue as normal, with no evidence so far that personal data was compromised.

The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has confirmed that a cyber incident that forced several online services offline was a deliberate attack.

The department said it detected an attempt to gain unauthorized access to its systems late Thursday. Several services, including online portals for state pensions, Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment (PIP), were taken offline as a precaution. Some remained unavailable as of 5 p.m. local time (1700 GMT) on Saturday.

The DWP said in a statement on X that it was working with the UK's National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to "bring services back online as soon as possible" while investigating how the attackers had attempted to access its systems.

Officials said there was no evidence that personal information had been compromised.

Pension and welfare payments continued as normal despite the disruption to online services. The department also said it had immediately activated established contingency plans in response to the incident.

UK faces growing number of cyberattacks

The attack is the latest in a series of cyber incidents affecting British public institutions and businesses.

In recent years, cyberattacks have disrupted operations at the British Library, Transport for London and major retailers including Marks & Spencer, Jaguar Land Rover and the Co-op, according to Reuters and AFP.

Earlier this month, cyberattacks targeting software used by supermarkets across Europe disrupted operations at several UK meat suppliers. Fashion retailers Next and Asos have also separately reported incidents involving unauthorized access to data.

A cyberattack in August targeted three British airports belonging to the Manchester Airports Group, resulting in the theft of personal data of 8.7 million customers.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre warned earlier this month that the country should prepare for the possibility of AI-powered cyberattacks targeting critical national infrastructure in the next two years.

Downing Street said on Friday, November 27, that there was no evidence other government departments had been targeted in the cyberattack, according to DPA news agency. A government source told the agency that investigations into the attack and those responsible were ongoing.

The UK's Information Commissioner's Office, the data protection watchdog, said it was in contact with the DWP about the incident.

UK warns of Russian sabotage threats

The cyberattack comes amid a wider wave of disruptions affecting businesses and public institutions, including Microsoft and the US Federal Aviation Administration in recent weeks.

Separately, Britain's domestic intelligence service MI5 and the Ministry of Defence this week warned UK military suppliers to Ukraine about an increase in Russian sabotage attempts.

The government issued guidance on identifying and reporting suspicious activity and reducing the risk of attacks.

US civil rights group challenges ICE subpoenas as attack on speech

The ACLU lawsuit claims subpoenas violate First Amendment rights by targeting anonymous dissenters of ICE policies.

The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticising its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights lawyers have claimed.

A federal class action filed on Friday, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), seeks a court order enjoining the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security from conducting a “bad-faith investigation” that violates the anonymous individuals’ First Amendment free speech rights.

The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) investigators.

ACLU lawyers sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case’s unsealing on Wednesday.

Boasberg scheduled a January 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU’s request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until December 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU’s allegations.

Spokespeople for DHS and US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office in Washington did not immediately respond to The Associated Press’s requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU’s lawsuit.

ACLU lawyers say Pirro’s office has used the term “Investigation 18” to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information.

“The investigation,” the ACLU says, “is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters.”

The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the “first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.”

“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” Laura Moraff, staff lawyer with the ACLU, said in a statement. “The First Amendment guarantees our right to criticize the government, including anonymously, and no one should fear being investigated for disagreeing with the president. This crackdown on dissent is antithetical to our nation’s core values.”

The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says.

The civil rights organisation says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas — a more secretive process — after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies.

The ACLU lawsuit’s plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: “Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth.” Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump.

“Defendants’ rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters,” ACLU lawyers wrote.

Laura Follansbee, staff lawyer with the ACLU of DC, claimed the use of grand jury subpoenas was “an alarming abuse of power”.

“The use of subpoenas to punish social media users for their speech is chilling not only for our clients but for others who fear being targeted because of their political beliefs,” Follansbee said.

Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected

Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.

Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty. The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.

After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine".

Attorney General for England and Wales, Ellie Reeves, who presented the UK's legal arguments in Hamburg earlier this month, told the BBC the ruling was "really significant" and an "a clear win for the UK government".

Earlier, in a joint statement with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, Reeves urged Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory: "Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt."

The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law, arguing that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.

The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.

The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.

Buenos Aires disagreed, writing in a statement after the decision that "Argentina did not ask the court to rule on sovereignty", but to apply the United Nations' sea laws to the UK over its "exploitation of our resources".

It also said that five individuals would face sanctions for their involvement in the oil drilling venture, something Milei had been threatening. The statement did not specify who the sanctions would be against.

"The message is clear: those who participate in the illegal exploitation of our resources will face the consequences," the statement said.

Professor Marc Weller, from the Chatham House think tank, told the BBC Argentina's legal challenge had "provisionally, but spectacularly, fallen at its first hurdle".

"While this is only a ruling in a preliminary phase of the case which may be heard more fully by an arbitral tribunal next year, this outcome casts doubts on the viability of the Argentina's claim in those proceedings," he added.

The 10-week war that was fought in 1982 started when Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim over the islands, as a British military task force fought to eject them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Despite its defeat, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falklands, and over the years, successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.

The UK government has made clear that sovereignty remains with Britain and maintains that the island's population has a right to self-determination.

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

Afghanistan: Several killed in blast near middle school

November 28, 2026

An explosion near a school in eastern Afghanistan has killed at least 10 students and injured 110 people. Officials say explosives at a nearby mining depot ignited due to negligence. An investigation is ongoing.

An explosion near a middle school in eastern Afghanistan's Kunar province on Saturday killed at least 10 students and injured 110 other people, most of them children, according to the Interior Ministry.

Authorities said a preliminary investigation indicated that the blast was caused by negligent storage of explosives at a depot near the school belonging to a mining company in the Andir Sir area of the provincial capital, Asadabad.

Deputy government spokesman Hamdullah Fitrat said initial findings pointed to "negligence and carelessness" at the depot. The explosion occurred at around 10 a.m. local time (05:30 a.m. UTC), according to earlier statements by provincial police officials.

Provincial officials warned that the number of casualties could increase. Unverified video footage posted on social media showed injured children being taken to the provincial hospital.

Samiulhaq Haqbayan, provincial director for information, told Germany's DPA news agency that the explosives were intended for use in mining operations and for clearing hazardous rocks from mountain slopes along the nearby Kunar-Nuristan highway.

Children among the injured

A school employee told AFP news agency that the explosion triggered panic among pupils.

"It was around 10 o'clock in the morning when an explosion erupted from that house, followed by screams of schoolchildren," said Latifullah, who declined to give his family name. "People scattered in every direction," he said.

An AFP journalist at a hospital in Asadabad reported injured children aged between eight and 15 being treated. Aliurahman, a local resident who helped transport victims to hospital, described seeing wounded children lying on the ground.

Abdullah, whose son was injured in the explosion, told AFP that the boy and his cousins had been trapped beneath a roof.

"My nephews are fine, but we took my son to the hospital, and thank God, he is doing better now," he said.

Third blast near a school this week

The ministry said an investigation into the incident is ongoing and further details will be announced once it is completed.

Saturday's incident is the third explosion near educational facilities in Afghanistan in the past week.

Two separate blasts near religious schools in Kapisa and Farah provinces killed a total of five students, with local officials attributing both incidents to unexploded ordinances left behind from previous conflicts.

EPA says initial tests show no toxic lead contamination in Iowa following detonation

Initial lab results from the controlled detonation of roughly five tons of unstable lead azide at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa showed no elevation of lead in water sources in the surrounding environment, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday.

"We will continue to provide updates in the coming days as new lab results for over 3,200 air, soil, dust and water samples (collected pre and post detonation) rapidly return and get validated," the agency wrote in a post on X.

The EPA says a team of 300 personnel and contractors spent the days immediately following Wednesday's blast collecting samples, in addition to monitoring for airborne lead for 30 consecutive hours.

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade or break down over time. It's especially dangerous to children and pregnant people, and experts say there is no safe level of exposure.

Military explosives experts detonated 68 drums of aging lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown after it was found to be at risk of spontaneous explosion. Residents within five miles of the plant were ordered to evacuate, and many others told to stay inside, amid fears of a toxic plume of the chemicals.

In the hours immediately after the explosion, U.S. Army officials called the detonation a success, saying that the mitigation measures put in place – including layers of contaminant and downward-facing explosives meant to drive the blast into the ground – had "exceeded expectations."

Still, many residents and some elected officials have criticized the military for a lack of transparency in the operation, including Iowa Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who has called for an investigation into why the lead azide was allowed to get to this precarious point.

"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," he said after the detonation. "Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared."

Sue Dyer, a corn and bean farmer about 18 miles southwest of the blast site, agreed that the biggest problem was communication, calling it "horrible."

"We didn't know anything about this until last week," she told NPR's Scott Simon in an interview on Saturday morning.

Dyer said that people in the community are all across the spectrum in terms of how worried they are after the detonation, even with reassurances from the federal government.

"Some people are sure that we're absolutely fine, and some people think we're absolutely dead. So put me somewhere in the middle until I have the data to make an opinion," she said, noting she is waiting for independent sampling results as well as those from the EPA.

Dyer says she had samples taken from her farmland before the blast and plans on taking her own samples again in the coming days, in hopes to get her farm verified lead-free.

"But what do you do if there's lead there?" Dyer asked. "I'm very hopeful that everything's fine, but I'm also a realist."

Argentina loses bid to stop Falklands oil project

Argentina vowed to continue its efforts to stop the British-Israeli oil project off the coast of the Falkland Islands after an international court rejected its request for a temporary block.

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) rejected on Saturday Argentina's bid to temporarily block oil drilling at the British-Israeli Sia Lion oil project off the UK-held Falkland Islands.

What did the judges rule?

At a special hearing in Hamburg, an independent court set up under UN auspices determined that Argentina's claims could not be resolved without first addressing the competing claims to sovereignty over the South Atlantic islands.

According to the judges, this question falls outside the scope of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that governs the world's oceans. Therefore, they rejected Argentina's claims by 18 votes to three.

The judges ruled that there was no reason to believe that the ITLOS had jurisdiction because it cannot make decisions based on questions of sovereignty.

However, Saturday's ruling was only preliminary, marking the start of what could be a long legal battle. The court urged both countries to swiftly establish the arbitration panel, which could still rule in Argentina's favor.

UK praises tribunal's ruling

"We welcome the decision by the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea not to prescribe provisional measures," United Kingdom Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said in a joint statement.

"The UK has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders," they added, urging Argentina to end its wider economic pressure.

In a 2013 referendum, more than 99% of the approximately 3,500 islanders voted to remain part of the United Kingdom. However, Argentina rejects this result.

How did Argentina react?

Meanwhile, Argentina vowed to continue its efforts to halt a British-Israeli oil project near the Falkland Islands.

"This decision is not the final word," President Javier Milei said in a statement, adding that Argentina will continue to "assert its rights through all diplomatic, legal and administrative channels at its disposal."

Milei also vowed to continue punishing companies working on the oil project, calling it a "clear and present danger" to Argentina's claims over the islands.

Argentine-UK conflict over Falklands reignites

The dispute between Britain and Argentina over the planned drilling dates back to their 10-week war over the South Atlantic islands which have been under British rule since 1833.

In 1982, Argentina's military junta invaded the Falkland Islands (known as the Islas Malvinas in Argentina). The subsequent conflict resulted in the deaths of 649 Argentine troops, 255 British troops, and three islanders.

In 2013, the Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining British. However, Argentina rejected the outcome. The country argues that the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers to have been implanted by Britain after 1833.

Dozens killed in Myanmar military strikes on wedding venue and school

Air strikes by Myanmar's military have killed dozens of people across the South East Asian nation, including at a wedding venue and a school.

Rescuers said at least 21 were confirmed dead, and at least 35 others injured, at the wedding site in Moe Bye village, in the country's southern Shan state, on Saturday afternoon.

On Thursday at least 20 civilians were killed, including students, young monks and teachers, when an air strike hit a school at In Yon village, in central Myanmar's Magway region where resistance forces are active, according to Myanmar's exiled National Unity Government (NUG).

Myanmar's military-led government has not commented on the strikes.

The military also carried out air strikes in Mrauk-U town, in western Myanmar's Rakhine state, on Saturday evening.

At about 20:00 local time (13:30 GMT), a residential area in the town was bombed, reportedly killing more than 10 people and injuring about 20 others.

The area is controlled by the Arakan Army (AA) - one of the strongest ethnic armies fighting the country's military regime.

Military air strikes have been happening almost daily across the country since a coup in 2021 toppled the elected civilian government led by former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, resulting in a lengthy civil war.

Villages have been burned and ground offensives have been carried out by the military on areas it is unable to control, including territories controlled by the NUG and ethnic armed organisations.

The latest strikes come a week after Myanmar was found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

A 2017 military crackdown killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee, but Myanmar denied committing genocide - saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The verdict marked the first time a state had ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

item.title: Symmetry shortcut narrows the search for hidden magnetic patterns
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

November 28, 2026 report

In some magnetic materials, the spins of individual atoms line up in highly ordered patterns but point in directions that almost completely cancel out, leaving the material unmagnetized. The exact arrangement of these spins can strongly affect how electrons move through a material, shaping both its electrical and magnetic properties. But because a single crystal can support such a huge number of plausible spin patterns, it would be impossible to test them one at a time.

Two independent research teams have now revealed how this search could be dramatically narrowed down. One team was led by Qihang Liu at the Southern University of Science and Technology in China, and the other by Takuya Nomoto at Tokyo Metropolitan University in Japan. Using differing methods, both teams have reproduced the known spin patterns of real magnets with strikingly different crystal structures.

Both studies have been published in Physical Review X.

Impossible search

While the arrangement of atoms in a crystal can be easily worked out, its magnetic structure is far harder to pin down and usually requires specialized measurements such as neutron diffraction. Researchers usually interpret these measurements using standard symmetry methods, which work out which spin patterns fit the shape of the crystal.

However, these methods often leave key details unresolved, such as the angles between neighboring spins or whether equivalent atoms carry spins of equal strength. In recent years, physicists have shown that treating rotations of the spins separately from the symmetry of the crystal itself can reveal patterns that would be missed by conventional methods.

Building on this idea, Liu's and Nomoto's teams each questioned whether crystal symmetry could narrow the search even further. To do this, the two groups first generated manageable lists of candidate patterns, then ranked them with computer simulations in two stages. First, they compared how the spins lined up relative to each other. Then they brought in spin–orbit coupling to work out how the favored patterns were oriented within the crystal.

Two different approaches

From here, the two teams diverged in their approaches. In their study, Liu's team searched for patterns repeating over regions up to four times the size of the crystal's basic building block, without having to specify the repeat length in advance. They then reproduced the known spin patterns in three very different magnets: a straight-line arrangement in MnTe, a triangular pattern in Mn₃Sn and a fully 3D arrangement in CoNb₃S₆. In a broader test, they recovered the reported magnetic structures for 73% of 1,178 materials screened.

In their own study, Nomoto's team sped up the second stage by reusing the arrangement of electrons calculated in the first round. They found that the observed pattern came out lowest in energy in 83% of 271 cases where the repeat length was already known.

Looking ahead, the two teams now hope to run stronger tests, making predictions from crystal structures measured before magnetic order sets in—before comparing them with later diffraction measurements. If successful, their approach could ultimately open up new routes to finding materials for spin-based memory and electronics.

How learning on the land is bringing back traditional food knowledge and healing

A viral 2017 poll claimed that 7% of American adults believe chocolate milk comes from brown cows. The results drew a lot of laughs, along with criticism of the poll's accuracy. But nearly a decade later, the results still raise an important question: How much do people really know about where their food comes from and how it's grown?

Grocery prices are skyrocketing in Canada amid a series of crises, from the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic to global conflict, climate change and cyberattacks on grocery chains.

As these events disrupt food supplies, it's time to revisit a skill set humans have valued for millennia—food literacy. Knowing how to grow, harvest, hunt, process and cook our own food can help us become more self-sufficient, and it starts with learning from the land.

Our disconnection from food

The disconnect between the food we eat and the land can be explained by the concept of distancing. It also involves complex power dynamics, financing and entities in the global food system that make our food hard to understand.

Distancing shapes how we value our food, the Earth and the people who work in the food system. Indigenous scholars Linda Clarkson and Vern Morrissette, along with Gabriel Régallet, argue that when we are separated from the source of our sustenance, we lose sight of "our responsibility and our kinship to the Earth." In essence, we collectively forget our responsibilities to the land.

For many Indigenous communities, food can no longer serve as medicine in the way it once did because colonization and the residential school system turned it into a tool of control. These systems forcibly disrupted intergenerational knowledge transfer, removed people from their lands, stigmatized traditional food and knowledge and ruptured relationships that had sustained people for generations.

While many initiatives now offer students and adults opportunities to learn traditional food knowledge, these efforts are not yet mainstream.

Building resilience through land-based learning

One approach to addressing collective forgetting and reclaiming food knowledge is land-based learning, an Indigenous approach to teaching rooted in understanding the land as a teacher. In our ongoing project, "Countering Collective Forgetting: The Role of Land Based Learning," we showcase the important work of those who teach these skills and how they are often undervalued.

Through hands-on teaching, land-based learning encourages adaptive knowledge often gained through the wisdom of Elders. Our research team recently reviewed 137 land-based learning studies. We found that Elder-led mentorship was the most prevalent approach to learning, appearing in 73% of the studies.

To showcase how land-based learning works in practice, we conducted our study on the unceded territories of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish) and shíshálh (Sechelt) Nations in an area commonly known as the Sunshine Coast of British Columbia. This region is particularly vulnerable to drought, and residents rely on ferry services for 60% of their food, with 40% coming from private barges and transport.

We participated in five land-based learning activities, hosted one learning circle and interviewed eight local land-based learning practitioners. These practitioners included seed savers, farmers, permaculturalists, Indigenous Knowledge Keepers, chefs, schoolteachers and outdoor educators. They comprised a mix of Indigenous and settler residents in their communities.

Our initial findings suggest that food acts as a form of living memory, held and reproduced through stories, relationships and also through engaging with the land.

The land is a teacher, healer

During our learning circle, Alfonso Salinas, a shíshálh educator and cultural ambassador, opened the session with a song and prayer. He described how he was "taken under the wings" of Elders and of shíshálh Nation educator Candace Campo (xets'emits'a), co-founder of Talaysay Tours, a local Indigenous land-based learning and tourism company.

On forest walks, Salinas learned how to use traditional plants and cedar as medicine. He shared his concerns about climate change and how invasive species are increasingly outcompeting native plants such as salmonberries. His message was to never forget to teach the history of the land.

One important piece of history shared by educators from the Sunshine Coast Seed Saving Collective during a seed workshop in September 2025 was that of the Japanese internment camps.

They helped people remember and honor survivors by planting Slocan peas.

Slocan peas are connected to Japanese Canadian families who were interned in the interior of British Columbia during World War II. Slocan peas grew through a period of injustice, carrying a memory of adaptation and resilience. Growing them is a form of healing.

One educator who identified as Red River Métis shared that it's hard to learn from the land when colonial policies continue to create barriers for Indigenous peoples. Zoning rules, the reserve system and resource extraction projects all stand in the way.

Finally, while many of the practitioners volunteered their time out of love, they also recognized this approach isn't sustainable.

Cost was a significant barrier for Robin, a settler who runs farm camps where kids from kindergarten to 12th grade can learn how to grow, process and cook food. She said it was difficult to balance the need to create more affordable land-based learning programs while ensuring that practitioners can continue to teach. "Land-based educators should be paid fair wages," she said.

Supporting traditional food knowledge

Seeds, like knowledge, don't stay viable forever. They have to be planted, harvested, saved and shared for the cycle to continue.…

Plant-inspired adhesive joins tiny blood vessels without stitches

Sewing together a blood vessel just a millimeter wide is delicate work. The connection must withstand each pulse while limiting damage to the vessel's inner lining. A new adhesive inspired by plant roots offers another approach. In rats, it cut the average joining time from about 39 minutes to less than nine while preserving a smoother passage for blood.

The material combines water-repelling glue with microscopic anchors that grip tissue, and an embedded battery-free wireless sensor can monitor a repaired vessel's pulse or the beating of a transplanted heart.

Researchers including Wen Zeng of Third Military Medical University in China and Malcolm Xing of the University of Manitoba describe the system in the journal Science. If clinically validated, the system could simplify small-vessel connections during transplantation and reconstructive surgery.

Anchoring in wet tissue

Previous adhesives have been largely ineffective in wet or blood-filled surgical settings. A film of water can prevent surgical glue from forming a strong bond with tissue. Adhering to blood vessels poses another challenge because they repeatedly expand and contract.

"The core of our innovation is a plant root–inspired design that enables robust adhesion in wet, dynamic conditions where traditional adhesives fail," the researchers write.

Their new silicone-based adhesive displaces surface water and forms chemical bonds with tissue. Embedded within it are tiny, 3D-printed anchors with four needlelike arms. These interlock with the vessel wall, much as roots anchor a plant in wet soil.

A temporary cuff supports and aligns the vessel ends during joining. The procedure keeps the adhesive outside the inner channel that carries blood, limiting the risk of the glue entering circulation.

Tests in rat carotid arteries that were approximately 1 millimeter across showed that the faster speed of the procedure resulted in less bleeding and preserved more of the vessels' delicate inner lining than conventional stitching.

Ten months after surgery, comparisons in small groups of rats found less thickening of the inner wall and more even blood flow at the adhesive joins than at the stitched ones. Excessive wall thickening can narrow an artery and compromise circulation.

A repair that can report back

The embedded wireless sensor adds a way to check the repair after surgery. Secured around a vessel, it responds to the wall's tiny movements with each pulse. Those movements change its electrical response, which an external reader detects without the need for an implanted battery.

To test the sensor, the researchers deliberately narrowed rat arteries to varying degrees. As the restriction increased, pulse signals weakened and changed shape. Machine-learning analysis used those changes to identify the narrowed vessels.

In a separate experiment, the team connected donor hearts to blood vessels in rats' necks. Sensors attached to the transplanted hearts recorded their beating over three months. Signal strength and rhythm helped distinguish functioning grafts from failing ones. Ultrasound provided a comparison: Failing grafts had lost heart-wall motion, while functioning transplants continued contracting.

The system has so far been used to identify existing narrowing and graft dysfunction in animals. Further tests must establish how reliably it works across vessel sizes and surgical sites, and whether it can warn of complications early enough for treatment to protect a repair or save a graft. The researchers propose that in the future their adhesive might be used to repair nerves, attach tendons, or seal leaks around the brain or spinal cord.

Scientists may have discovered the hidden root cause of allergies

- Date:

November 28, 2026

- Source:

Griffith University

- Summary:

Scientists are challenging decades of medical thinking with a surprising hypothesis that allergies may begin with an energy failure inside the body's protective barrier cells rather than an overactive immune system. When these cells cannot cope with environmental stresses, they may trigger the immune reactions associated with eczema, food allergies, and other allergic conditions.

Researchers may have uncovered a previously overlooked biological cause of allergies that challenges decades of medical thinking. Instead of originating in the immune system, allergic diseases may begin with an energy failure inside the cells that form the body's protective barriers, including those lining the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus.

Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist at Griffith University's School of Medicine and Dentistry, led the research. His team examined what it believes to be the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data assembled to date, encompassing 116 case-control cohorts, 3,776 patients, and 2,164 cohorts. Multi-omic research combines different types of molecular data to provide a more comprehensive picture of the biological processes underlying disease.

The findings point to a potentially fundamental shift in how allergic diseases develop.

Rethinking the Origins of Allergies

"For 60 years, we've taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around," Professor Smith said.

"Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body's barrier surfaces.

"The barrier cell can't meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment, so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy follow.

"It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions."

Mitochondria are tiny structures inside cells that generate most of the energy needed for cellular functions. Epithelial cells depend on this energy to maintain the protective barriers that separate the body from its surroundings, repair damage, and respond to environmental threats. When these energy supplies become compromised, the cells may struggle to perform these essential functions properly.

Evidence of a Hidden Cellular Energy Crisis

The most compelling evidence supporting the hypothesis came from patients with eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic allergic condition that causes inflammation in the esophagus, the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach.

Across all 13 independent groups of patients with the condition, researchers identified reduced activity in the biological machinery responsible for removing damaged mitochondria. This cellular recycling process is known as mitophagy and is essential for maintaining a healthy population of functioning mitochondria.

The researchers also identified abnormalities in the skin's protective barrier and antioxidant defenses in people with eczema, even in areas of skin showing no signs of inflammation.

However, the same biological pattern did not appear consistently across all allergic diseases. Researchers found no evidence of the signature in established asthma or nasal polyps, while hay fever showed only partial evidence of the proposed mechanism.

Could Modern Life Be Fueling the Allergy Epidemic?

The researchers suggest that many seemingly unrelated risk factors for allergies may converge on a single biological vulnerability: the ability of protective barrier cells to generate enough energy to function properly.

Potential contributors include diets rich in processed foods, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and exposure to antibiotics early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a study co-author and molecular immunologist at Griffith University's School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences, explained that allergic diseases have long been associated with a wide range of possible causes. However, a single biological explanation capable of accounting for the dramatic increase in allergies within just one generation has remained elusive.

The proposed mechanism may also offer an explanation for why allergic diseases frequently return despite successful treatment.

"The research also explains why allergies can relapse," Associate Professor West said.

"Once inflammation is established, it damages the barrier further.

"Today's drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause."

In other words, if the researchers are correct, allergic inflammation could create a damaging cycle in which weakened barrier cells trigger an immune response, and that response further compromises the protective barrier.

Searching for the Root Cause of Allergies

Professor Smith emphasized that the research presents a hypothesis that requires further testing rather than a definitively established explanation for allergic disease. Nevertheless, it provides researchers with a promising new direction for investigating how allergies first develop.

"We have spent our careers managing the smoke, and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking," he said.

"This is not a cure but is something we have never had before -- a logical starting point.

"The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops."…

Yale researchers have discovered that moderate calorie restriction reduces an immune protein linked to aging and chronic inflammation, apparently independently of weight loss. Blocking this protein could potentially mimic some of the benefits of eating less and help people stay healthier for longer.

Their discovery centers on an immune system protein that helps protect the body from infections but may also contribute to chronic inflammation as we grow older.

Reducing calorie intake has been shown to extend lifespan in several animal species, including mice, rhesus monkeys, and fruit flies. In some cases, these animals also remain free of disease for longer. However, extreme calorie restriction can come at a significant biological cost. Mice that consume 40% fewer calories, for example, become more vulnerable to infections, experience impaired growth, and are less likely to reproduce.

Researchers have long sought a way to harness the potential longevity benefits of calorie restriction in humans without these harmful consequences. In a new study published in Nature Aging, Yale scientists identified a promising target: an immune system protein known as complement component 3 (C3).

Earlier research from Yale demonstrated that people who reduced their calorie intake by a moderate 14% over two years experienced improvements in immune defense without sacrificing growth or reproductive function.

"This concept demonstrates that aging is actually malleable and a process that can be targeted," says senior author Vishwa Deep Dixit, PhD, Waldemar Von Zedtwitz Professor of Pathology, professor of immunobiology and of comparative medicine, and director of the Yale Center for Research on Aging (Y-Age) at Yale School of Medicine.

Eating Less Reduces a Protein Linked to Aging

The trial, known as CALERIE, stands for Comprehensive Assessment of Long-Term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy.

Over the course of the trial, participants successfully lowered their calorie consumption by 11% to 14% without experiencing a sense of deprivation.

By examining blood samples collected over time, the scientists identified more than 7,000 proteins. One particularly intriguing finding was that levels of C3 fell significantly in response to calorie restriction.

C3 is a central component of the complement system, a network of proteins that helps the immune system recognize and eliminate potentially harmful invaders, including bacteria. Although this system is essential for protecting the body, excessive activation may have damaging consequences.

Previous research has linked complement system activity to chronic inflammation, a persistent inflammatory response that can damage healthy tissues over time. Chronic inflammation is considered a major hallmark of biological aging and contributes to the development of numerous age-related diseases.

"But the causal effects of C3 in aging and chronic inflammation have not been identified. So, we were very excited to find that in our study," says Hee-Hoon Kim, PhD, a postdoctoral associate in the Dixit lab and a co-first author of the paper.

By comparing protein levels at the beginning and end of the two-year calorie restriction period, the researchers pinpointed white adipose tissue as the primary tissue affected by the dietary intervention. White adipose tissue is the most abundant type of body fat in mammals. Beyond storing energy, it plays important roles in metabolism, hormone production, and immune function.

The researchers then turned to mice to investigate the biological mechanisms behind their findings. Consistent with observations in humans, C3 expression increased as the animals aged.

Further biochemical experiments revealed an unexpected source of this increase: visceral white adipose tissue. Visceral fat accumulates deep within the abdomen, surrounding internal organs, and has been associated with chronic inflammation and metabolic disease.

Using a technique called single-cell RNA sequencing, which allows scientists to examine gene activity within individual cells, the team traced the production of C3 to specific populations of macrophages associated with aging that reside within fat tissue.

"This whole process was unknown in the beginning," Mishra says.

Macrophages are white blood cells that form part of the body's first line of immune defense.

The discovery raised an important question: Could people benefit from lower C3 activity without having to lose weight?

Scientists create stunning, non-fading paint without a single pigment

- Date:

November 28, 2026

- Source:

Kobe University

- Summary:

Researchers have developed a pigment-free coating that delivers the rich, glossy appearance of automotive paint without the problem of fading. Inspired by nature, the technology uses microscopic silicon spheres to produce durable colors that remain consistent from different viewing angles. The coating is so lightweight that the color layer for an entire passenger airliner could theoretically weigh less than a carton of milk.

Researchers at Kobe University have developed a coating that produces the rich colors and glossy finish of automotive paint without relying on pigments. The breakthrough overcomes several major limitations of structural color, making it possible to apply colors that resist fading to large, complex surfaces, maintain a consistent hue from different viewing angles, and add protective coatings.

"Color coatings are expected to provide vivid color, brightness, gloss, and long-term durability, yet no existing technology satisfies all of these requirements simultaneously," says Kobe University materials engineer Hiroshi Sugimoto.

Traditional paints typically require relatively thick layers of pigments, which add considerable weight and can fade over time. Structural color, a phenomenon responsible for the brilliant appearance of peacock feathers, offers an alternative that avoids the fading caused by light exposure in organic pigments. However, conventional approaches to structural color require precisely arranged microscopic structures, often produce different colors depending on the viewing angle, and are incompatible with protective coatings.

Unlocking Glossy Color Without Pigments

Sugimoto previously pioneered a new method of producing structural color using tiny silicon spheres that generate consistent colors regardless of viewing angle. His team subsequently adapted the technology for inkjet printing (link). Although the resulting coatings produced color successfully, they scattered reflected light in multiple directions, leaving their surfaces without a glossy finish. The technique that made inkjet printing possible, however, also provided a potential solution to this problem.

Sugimoto explains, "Packing the nanospheres in silica shells not only protects the particles but also controls their spacing and should improve self-assembly into neat arrays." Arranging the particles more uniformly reduces the scattering of reflected light, allowing the coating to develop a glossy appearance.

In a study published in the journal Small Structures, the researchers demonstrated that they could produce and adjust the gloss of structural color coatings on large, three-dimensional surfaces. They also found that applying a protective layer had little effect on the resulting color.

"The most exciting aspect of this work is that it demonstrates glossy, non-iridescent and protection-coated structural color coatings for 3D objects in a single platform, making the technology useful for real-world applications," explains Sugimoto.

Ultra-Lightweight Paint Could Transform Aviation

One of the technology's most remarkable advantages is its extremely low weight. A single layer of silicon nanospheres is sufficient to produce bright colors with high opacity, effectively concealing the underlying surface.

The potential weight savings are particularly striking for aviation. Conventional coatings on wide-body airliners currently add several hundred kilograms to the aircraft's weight. The researchers estimate that a color coating based on their technology could weigh only several hundred grams, less than a carton of milk for an entire airplane.

The materials used to create these coatings also offer environmental advantages. Silicon is nontoxic and can be sourced from the semiconductor industry, while silica is among the most abundant materials in Earth's crust. Combined with their resistance to fading, the minimal material requirements could make future color coatings significantly less resource-intensive.

Taking Structural Color Beyond Paint

Sugimoto is helping establish a company to increase production and bring the technology to industrial markets. The coating process is particularly promising because it can be integrated into several established manufacturing techniques.

"The process is compatible with scalable coating methods such as spray coating, slot-die coating, and roll-to-roll processing."

Beyond commercial paint applications, Sugimoto hopes to use the underlying science to create advanced coatings that perform multiple functions. Future versions could combine vivid structural color with capabilities related to sensing, light-driven chemical reactions, and energy management.

He says: "We want to expand the possibility of applications for the science behind our technology beyond coloration. Looking ahead, we aim to develop multifunctional silicon nanoparticle coatings that combine structural coloration with additional optical functions such as sensing, photocatalysis, and energy management."

There are many oddities out in space—as David Bowie foretold—and astronomers have just discovered yet another: a triple-star system some 28 light-years from Earth that shouldn’t really exist in its current form.

For decades, experts thought this system contained only two star remnants. The data showed a red dwarf (the smallest type of hydrogen-burning star, significantly smaller than the sun) being orbited by a very distant white dwarf (the burnt-out remnants of a dead star, typically about the size of Earth).

Read more: “Did Astronomers Finally Witness a Black Hole Eat a White Dwarf for the First Time?”

What was hiding was another white dwarf much closer to the central red dwarf star. A reanalysis that started in 2019—and has now been published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics—offers clues as to what exactly this unusual stellar system has in it. “We were actually looking for planets,” study author Étienne Artigau said in a statement. “Instead, we found something much more surprising.”

The velocity changes of the red dwarf suggested that something with much more mass than an exoplanet was pulling on it, which is how the white dwarf was uncovered. While these white dwarf remnants are the size of Earth, they’re about 200,000 times heavier—entire stars crushed down into (relatively) tiny specks.

Why is all of this so unexpected?

Before this inner white dwarf became a white dwarf, it would’ve ballooned in size, becoming around 40 percent bigger than the sun. Under normal circumstances, that would have pulled in the red dwarf and swallowed it up. But somehow, the red dwarf beat the odds and is still there—though it’s not clear how. “The system should not exist,” study author Patrick Dufour said. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”

The new triple-star system has been given the name Welopōʻai, which means “path of family traits” in Hawaiian—an acknowledgement to the two telescopes that made the discovery, both located on Maunakea on the Big Island.

It promises to be of great value in studying how different types of stars and their inner structures evolve, and how matter reacts when under extreme densities. After all, it’s the closest triple-star system including two white dwarfs that’s ever been discovered, and there’s no other system like it within 100 light-years of Earth.

Why a common cold can trigger an asthma flare: A single protein may fuel two kinds of inflammation

A common cold can quickly trigger an asthma episode, with respiratory viruses such as rhinovirus being among the most common culprits. During these viral flare-ups, levels of G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) rise in the body. This growth factor protein regulates the production, release and survival of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell that helps fight infections. A recent study investigated how the single protein G-CSF acts as a master driver of severe lung inflammation during viral asthma flare-ups and whether blocking it could lead to a powerful new treatment.

The researchers tracked daily respiratory symptoms, lung capacity and G-CSF levels in 28 asthma patients and 11 healthy control participants, then experimentally inoculated them with rhinovirus A16, the common cold virus, as the disease progressed.

When infected with the common cold virus, rhinovirus, asthma patients experienced a sharp surge in G-CSF levels, an increase that was absent in healthy individuals. This rise in G-CSF was accompanied by stronger inflammatory responses and higher amounts of the virus. Across the human cohort, greater G-CSF gene activity was also associated with more severe lower-airway symptoms, although it did not correspond to larger declines in lung function.

These findings were published in Science Translational Medicine.

Double whammy of inflammation

Sudden asthma flare-ups account for most asthma-related hospitalizations and are most commonly triggered by respiratory viruses such as rhinovirus. Allergic asthma is traditionally viewed as a type 2 inflammatory disease driven by eosinophils, a type of white blood cell. However, viral infections complicate this picture, triggering both type 2 and neutrophilic inflammation in the lungs at the same time.

The standard treatment for acute flare-ups relies heavily on oral corticosteroids. While the steroids effectively suppress type 2 allergic inflammation, the same cannot be said about their effects on neutrophilic inflammation. This led scientists to investigate whether a single biological switch could be driving both inflammatory responses during viral infections.

They turned their attention to G-CSF, which is known to control the production and survival of neutrophils. Recent studies had also begun to hint that G-CSF could fuel type 2 allergic inflammation by acting on other immune cells, although the evidence was not yet strong enough to establish this role.

In search of what drives the flare-ups both ways, the team collected bronchial brushings and bronchoalveolar fluid at baseline and on day 4 post-infection, along with nasal lavage samples across days 0 to 10. For 14 days, they monitored daily lower and upper respiratory symptoms as well as lung function, G-CSF gene and protein levels, viral load, neutrophils and type 2 allergic cytokines. To examine the underlying cellular mechanisms, female mice were sensitized to an allergen to simulate allergic asthma and then infected intranasally with rhinovirus.

Protein holds the key

The experiments revealed that G-CSF does more than regulate neutrophils. It can also directly fuel type 2 allergic inflammation by activating allergic immune cells, including ILC2s, dendritic cells and CD4+ TH2 cells. This, in turn, boosts the production of allergic cytokines, along with eosinophils. They also found that giving recombinant G-CSF to allergic mice was enough on its own to trigger a full-blown asthma flare-up.

The next step was to see if blocking G-CSF could stop both inflammatory responses from spiraling out of control during a viral flare-up. The researchers found that mice treated with a G-CSF-blocking antibody had fewer neutrophils and allergic immune cells crowding their lungs and airways. The treatment also eased airway stiffness and breathing resistance in mice, while preventing tissue damage and excessive mucus buildup.

The findings make a case for blocking G-CSF to treat asthma attacks triggered by the cold virus. The researchers, however, noted one important limitation. In the mouse studies, G-CSF-blocking treatment was given just before virus exposure, whereas in real life, treatment would likely begin after an asthma attack has started. They suggest that future studies could test the treatment at this stage to make the findings more clinically relevant.

When trying to understand a new situation or scenario, humans usually try to work out connections between the different elements involved. If they recognize a familiar pattern, they can use mental connections established from past experiences to guide their interpretation and decisions.

The ability to infer relationships in new situations based on overall patterns is referred to as structure-based inference. It can be very useful, as it helps people to adapt their world interpretations in changing and unfamiliar circumstances.

Researchers at the University of Oxford recently carried out a study aimed at better understanding how the brain supports structure-based inference. Their paper, published in Nature Human Behaviour, suggests that a brain region called the hippocampus, which is central to the encoding and retrieval of memories, helps people to use previously learned relationships to make sense of new situations.

"Our study was motivated by two simple questions: how do we learn the underlying structure behind our experiences, and how do we use that knowledge to make inferences in new situations?" Deng Pan, first author of the paper, told Medical Xpress.

"In everyday life, we rarely learn everything from scratch. Instead, we recognize patterns across different experiences and use what we have learned before to understand something new. We wanted to understand how the human brain supports this ability, and particularly whether the hippocampus, a brain region important for learning and memory, plays a causal role in learning relational knowledge and using it to make inferences."

Assessing how people learn and infer relationships

To investigate the neural underpinnings of structure-based inference, Pan and his colleagues carried out a series of experiments in which participants played a game on a computer screen. The game they designed, called the Goalkeeper Game, required participants to learn the relationships between several players.

"The game allowed us to study how people recognize the 'structure' underlying these relationships and then use this knowledge to infer new ones," said Pan.

As 36 participants played the Goalkeeper Game on a computer, the researchers scanned their brains using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that tracks changes in blood oxygenation linked to brain activity. The team analyzed the collected scans to identify patterns representing the relationships between characters.

Subsequently, they also used computational models, including recurrent neural networks (RNNs), to investigate the processes supporting learning and inference.

"We combined several different approaches," explained Pan. "We used brain imaging to ask where this relational 'structure' is represented in the brain and found that the answer was the hippocampus. We built reinforcement learning models to understand participants' behavior, and RNNs to model the neural computations that might support this process."

In a follow-up experiment, the researchers noninvasively and temporarily modulated activity in the hippocampus of 20 participants before they started playing the game. They did this using a technique called transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS), which sends ultrasound waves through the skull.

"This allowed us to directly test whether the hippocampus causally contributes to learning relationships and making new inferences," said Pan.

The team observed that during the experiment, participants were able to infer relationships between players that they had not directly experienced, using previously learned connections to fill gaps in what they knew. Moreover, stimulating the hippocampus appeared to disrupt this ability to infer relationships based on learned connections.

"Although the whole study is important, I think the key contribution is that we provided causal evidence for the role of the hippocampus in high-level cognition in healthy humans," said Pan. "We believe this is a major step forward in how we study hippocampal function in healthy humans. This has traditionally been difficult because it required studying patients with hippocampal damage, while conventional noninvasive stimulation cannot easily reach the hippocampus deep inside the brain."

The promise of TUS for studying flexible learning

Using TUS, Pan and his colleagues were able to temporarily alter activity in the hippocampus, assessing the effects of this on people's behavior. In addition to uncovering the role of the hippocampus in structure-based inference, their study thus highlights the potential of TUS for conducting neuroscience and psychology research.

"We hope TUS could be a game changer for bridging the gap between high-level cognition, such as learning, inference and decision-making, and its neural basis in healthy humans, especially when these processes involve deep brain regions such as the hippocampus," said Pan. "For future research, I would like to use TUS to study a broader range of high-level cognitive functions that interest me. Many of these, such as problem-solving, reasoning and planning, are difficult to study in animals."

Pan is currently planning more experiments that will rely on TUS to temporarily alter people's brain activity. He thinks that the technique could be particularly useful for examining functions that are supported by regions situated deep inside the brain, which have proved difficult to study noninvasively.

"In the longer term, I would like to better understand the mechanisms of TUS neuromodulation and explore how it could be developed into noninvasive treatments for disorders involving deep brain regions," added Pan. "For example, this could include targeting hippocampal circuits involved in memory or amygdala-related circuits involved in emotion in conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)."…

Prioritize CVE-2026-133311 as part of an exploited MiCollab cluster

A vulnerability management queue can make CVE-2026-133311 look easy to defer. Mitel rates the MiCollab AWV issue 5.9, describes a high-complexity attack and limits the direct impact to sensitive information disclosure. The CVE alone does not receive a critical score. The surrounding evidence changes the priority. The same advisory contains command-execution issues, the five-CVE set has been exploited, and CISA ADP marks exploitation as active.

That is not an argument for treating every medium issue as critical. It is an argument for grouping related findings when the vendor and attackers treat them as a set. A patch program that ranks each CVE in isolation may postpone the authentication flaw while a critical sibling is remediated. If both are fixed by the same advisory and affect the same component, splitting the work can leave a prepared or partially patched path behind.

What belongs in the risk record

Record the CVE's own facts first. CVE-2026-133311 is CWE-1390 weak authentication, affects MiCollab through 10.3 (10.3.0.18), requires a specific generated identifier or pre-staged content, and can disclose sensitive information. The CVSS 3.1 vector is network reachable, high complexity, no privileges and no user interaction, with high confidentiality impact only. Mitel's patch for 10.3.0.18 or a later supported release is the remediation path.

Then record the portfolio context. MISA-2026-0012 includes CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133311, CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133324. The first, second, fourth and fifth cover upload, XML injection, command injection and authentication bypass. Mitel says exploiting them together can significantly amplify impact. CERT-In reports known exploitation. APEX Labs published an intrusion timeline and CISA KEV references.

The risk record should describe both levels. It should not claim that the medium CVE alone caused the critical outcome. It should explain why the same exposed component and patch cycle create a common remediation boundary.

Prioritization questions

Is the affected component reachable from the internet or from an untrusted partner network? Does the server integrate with Active Directory or store credentials for other systems? Is the version at or below 10.3.0.18? Has the vendor patch been verified rather than assumed from a build label? Are upstream logs available and retained long enough to investigate exploitation before the patch window?

If AWV is externally reachable and the version is unpatched, contain first and investigate immediately. If the component is not externally reachable, still apply the vendor fix and verify that no secondary path exists through a proxy or gateway. The CVSS score informs severity, but reachability, identity integration and known exploitation set the operational timeline.

Evidence that supports urgency

The CVE record's CISA ADP entry references the Accenture report and the KEV catalog, and its SSVC content marks exploitation as active. SecurityWeek reports that all five MiCollab flaws were added to KEV. APEX Labs observed a web shell before Mitel published the advisory and reported a second server communicating with the same actor infrastructure.

ZoomEye returned 730,707 matches for http.body="MiCollab" and zero matches for vul.cve="CVE-2026-133311". The page-body count indicates a broad searchable product presence, not a confirmed vulnerable population. It should not be used as a risk multiplier by itself. Internal inventory and version evidence are more defensible.

Remediation standard

Define completion as a supported patched build, verified on every production node, with all publication paths accounted for. Apply the 10.3.0.18 patch or move to a later release. Restrict external AWV access until validation is complete. Preserve evidence from systems that may have been compromised before the patch.

After remediation, review the LDAP connector and other reachable secrets. Examine proxy and identity logs for pre-patch activity. If the organization uses a KEV deadline, track the application patch and the incident investigation as separate workstreams. Closing the vulnerability ticket does not close a possible intrusion.

The priority statement should be concise: CVE-2026-133311 is a medium authentication flaw in an actively exploited multi-CVE MiCollab set. Remediate it with its sibling CVEs and treat exposed, unpatched servers as potential compromise cases.

Across South Asia and emerging education markets, the biggest barrier to quality university admission preparation is rarely a lack of motivation—it is friction.

Most commercial EdTech platforms follow a familiar playbook: require students to download a 120MB mobile app, create an account with phone verification, and hit a subscription paywall before they can check a single past-year question or eligibility rule. For a high-school student on a budget Android phone and an unstable 4G connection, that friction is often enough to make them give up.

While building Shikka.bd, an open-access university admission and 3D STEM learning hub, we tested the opposite approach: zero-login, sub-100ms web tools designed specifically for mobile-first students.

1. The Hidden Cost of "App-Only" Education

When a student searches Google at midnight for "DU admission negative marking rules" or "National University merit score calculation", they want an immediate, trustworthy answer—not an app store redirect.

Forcing an app install creates three problems:

- Storage & Data Overhead: Entry-level smartphones frequently run out of storage, causing students to uninstall heavy study apps between exams.

- Search Engine Invisibility: Content locked inside native apps cannot be indexed by search engines or screen readers, cutting off free organic discovery.

- Exclusion of Underserved Tracks: Commercial apps naturally prioritize high-margin engineering/medical coaching while neglecting massive student populations such as National University honours applicants.

2. Combining Static Speed with Interactive 3D STEM

Making a web platform fast does not mean stripping away interactivity. On Shikka.bd, we separated discoverable reference content from heavy simulation bundles:

- Instant Static Routes: Key guides—including the University Admission Eligibility Calculator, National University (NU) 200-Point Merit Hub, and past-year Question Bank—load directly from CDN edge HTML in under 100ms.

- Lazy-Loaded Interactive Visualizers: When a student opens a physics projectile simulation, a 3D biology model, or a geometric proof, the browser loads the Three.js and JSXGraph modules on demand without slowing down the initial page.

3. Designing for Trust and Accessibility

Students preparing for high-stakes exams need verified numbers, not guesses. Every formula, GPA threshold, and negative-marking rule should cite official university circulars clearly and work without requiring personal data or account sign-ups.

When EdTech teams remove login walls and optimize for sub-100ms web delivery, educational access expands immediately—especially for students who rely on shared devices or prepaid mobile data.

I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.

In an early PartySim build, adding a second drinks table took the simulated wait from three minutes to eight. The build passed.

Every year we throw a Halloween party for about 80 people. I built PartySim for it. Give it a floor plan and it builds a 3D haunted house full of simulated guests, so you can see where the party jams up.

I have a day job, so I set up Kiro Crew on my laptop to work through a queue while I was away. The jobs built changes, reviewed them and opened pull requests. I decided what got merged. Other people call this a software factory. For this project, we call it a haunted house.

the builds passed and the app was wrong

Early on I gave three models the same small feature. All three passed the build and linter. In the app, one worked, one was too faint to see, and one did nothing. Even the one that worked left this in its log:

Left undone: Visual verification at real size (server not started in this session)

The next night, three more features passed build and lint and still had problems I could see or hear in the app.

so the Grim Reaper looks at the app

For a visual change, the brief names one thing I should be able to see. A script opens the same URL and repeats the same clicks on the branch and on the commit where it split from main. The Grim Reaper reads the brief and the diff, then compares the screenshots. He writes PASS or FAIL with the screenshot and the file and line he checked. His agent is configured to write its findings in one folder:

{ "capability": "fs_write",

"match": ["docs/local/evidence/**"],

"effect": "allow" }

Back to the drinks table. Guests walking to a table didn't count toward its line, so too many picked the table that looked free. Pull request #6 counted guests on the way over and turned the table so its line ran onto the lawn. At the same minute of the same party, adding the second table now took the wait from three minutes down to two.

On another change, the brief asked for three lines of text to fit. They did. The extra line cut off the bottoms of the buttons below. The build and linter passed. The Reaper wrote FAIL.

who works in the haunted house

I handed Dracula a request or wrote the brief myself. Frankenstein, the Grim Reaper and the Ferryman ran on timers. They passed work through files and Git: a brief, a branch, screenshots and a review note. I handled the merge.

elsewhere in the house

The prompts and permissions live in .kiro/agents/. The roadmap is Markdown. For 102 of the 110 briefs in the build queue, we wrote out what to find and what to replace. That let me give Frankenstein the work on a small model at 0.06× Kiro credits.

what broke when I left it running

- When a Task Runner step failed, it ran a hard reset. That's why each build gets its own worktree.

- My first unattended jobs weren't allowed to read files. Each job needed its own tool allowlist.

- Jobs pause after two failures in a row. If I closed the laptop lid, the whole night shift stopped.

Between November 10 and 25, the Ferryman opened 103 pull requests. The PRs credit Frankenstein with 83 builds. Ninety-nine included screenshots, and 54 had a section for a screen that was supposed to stay the same.

I couldn't review them as fast as they came in. One evening I merged ten in the same second. I still have to work out how to give each one a proper look.

A screenshot also shows one moment. How do you test a queue that only starts backing up ten minutes into a simulation?

item.description:
