Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

How you can spot and avoid scam ads on social media

Convincing fake stores and AI-generated celebrity endorsements are making scam ads harder to recognize.

Imagine stumbling upon a Facebook ad for a jacket that's $300 under normal circumstances, going for a mere $39. With high-quality images and logos you recognize, plus a ticking clock to pressure you into buying within a short timeframe, these ads are often effective at getting you to act without thinking it through. But in most cases, that "bargain" is you handing over money to a fraudster.

Many people have fallen victim to scam ads on social media, some of which direct people to make a purchase from an external website. People reported losing over $95 million as a result of such purchases in 2025. Reported losses from all types of scams beginning on social media totaled $2.1 billion in the same year.

They may appear to be run by well-known and reputable businesses, sell nonexistent goods or feature fake celebrity endorsements (some created using AI). Many will direct you to a fake website, while others seek as many of your details as possible. As with most places online, having the word Sponsored simply means a fee has been paid to display the ad, so you need to investigate more to see whether it's legitimate.

Fake stores don't always look fake

Don't assume a phony site will be of poor quality and full of typos. Many scam ads will copy logos, images and their general look from the pages of well-known stores. Add large reductions with an offer counting down to "end of day", and they can be very convincing.

As recently as February 2026, Meta sued a Vietnam-based advertiser over a range of products purportedly available at reduced prices, including those of Longchamp. Shoppers completed a survey before reaching a site asking for credit card details. Meta said products were not delivered, but unauthorized recurring charges were made.

In separate cases, advertisers used manipulated images and voices of celebrities appearing to recommend healthcare products or lure victims into investment groups. With AI getting this good, classic giveaways like poor-quality images or awkward voiceovers aren't as common now.

The number of people affected by the Longchamp-style offers hasn't been disclosed. However, these are all good examples of how having the right logo and images, a well-produced clip with a celebrity or other recognizable features doesn't mean the source can be trusted.

Check the website, not just the discount

As a general rule, it's best to avoid clicking through to any website. Instead, type the name of the shop or store into a new tab and go directly to their homepage. This will help you avoid impersonator sites, though it's still possible to fall for a "discount" page that isn't claiming to be a well-known brand if you're not careful.

Look carefully at the URL, which may have additional or different words, spelling or domain ending to impersonate a genuine site. Try Googling the company name and "scam", "fraud" and similar words, and reading others' comments and experiences. Many fraudulent sites will use stock images or photos lifted from other companies, so it can also be worthwhile to do a reverse image search.

Don't assume that the presence of a padlock icon or "HTTPS" at the start of the URL means the company is reputable. HTTPS only encrypts your connection to the site, and scammers can use it too. A secure connection to a fraudulent site doesn't protect you from falling for it.

It's also useful to pause for a moment and apply some common sense. Always remember the old "too good to be true" line: luxury brands are not going to suddenly offer their goods at 80 percent off when the prestige is their main selling point.

If possible, you should always pay with a credit card (or wallet like PayPal) when buying from an unknown website, as that gives you more protection if you need to dispute any transactions. If you're asked to pay using unusual methods like gift cards or money transfers, you're almost certainly dealing with a scam. Gift card payments are a frequent tactic of scammers; legitimate companies won't ask you to pay with them.

Naturally, none of the above will be totally reliable indicators on their own every time. Still, it's well worth taking a short time to research a company before purchasing from them, rather than trying to get a refund or have a problem resolved for many weeks afterwards.

Clicked a scam ad? Here's what to do

In case you do open a shady website, don't enter your details or download any files. Double-check that nothing was downloaded, and decline any prompts to download programs. If something did get downloaded, don't open it. Delete it, then update and run an anti-malware scanner to make sure all is OK.

Entered a password or other details already? You should change those passwords, along with those for any other sites where you use the same password. If you've entered payment details, even if you didn't finish checking out, you should notify your bank or credit card company, explain what happened and ask them to prevent further payments. You can also ask them to reclaim any payments you made to the scam company.

Meta's page on fraudulent ads has links to report scam ads on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. TikTok's support also explains how to report an ad on that platform. Even after a report, you might see others like it, so keep your guard up.

It's also useful to take screenshots of the ad. Keep the URL of the website and details of any payments made, if they happened. You can report fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Even with Google Maps features that work better on Android Auto vs. CarPlay, you might prefer another navigation app. Whether you have good reason to dislike Google Maps because of the way it works or you simply want something else to try, Android Auto supports alternatives like Waze, HERE WeGo, TomTom, MapQuest and Magic Earth. These apps look a bit different and offer distinct advantages, from privacy-focused features to offline maps and cleaner interfaces.

Sometimes, Google Maps won't do for driving in certain cities. It might work brilliantly for driving in New York City, for instance, but poorly in another part of the world. User numbers can also make a difference: more drivers using a crowdsourced navigation app can help improve its routing, as with Waze. Or maybe you're looking for a different app because you don't trust Google with your driving info. Or you might simply prefer how another app looks and works more than Google Maps. At the end of the day, that's exactly what matters most.

Waze

Waze built its reputation on community-powered traffic data and that continues to be its biggest draw. There are tons of reports from drivers about accidents, speed traps, police presence, road closures and real-time traffic jams. If you were avoiding Google Maps because you don't want all your data in Google's hands, then you're out of luck because Waze is owned by the tech giant. Still, there's no denying that there are some benefits to this, because the app uses Gemini-powered Conversational Reporting. This way, you can speak naturally about what you saw rather than take your eyes off the road to report an issue.

Waze also provides a cool feature called personalized navigation, which suggests routes based on your past trips, and a less chatty mode that trims down voice prompts while keeping essential turn alerts intact. Spend five minutes exploring the hidden features every Waze user should know about, and you will see you can change a ton of things, from how your car shows up on the map to the voice guiding you. Or maybe you want Christina Aguilera to tell you when to turn left, or you want to hear dad jokes while you drive. It's all in there.

You should know, however, that Waze doesn't really support offline navigation. An already-loaded route may keep working if you briefly lose data, but you can't download offline maps. You might also find the screen to be cluttered with alerts popping up constantly, which can be annoying if your car's infotainment screen is on the smaller side.

Here WeGo

Here WeGo takes a different approach to leading you places, leaning on frequently updated maps and decent global coverage rather than Waze-style community reports. It works with Android Auto for turn-by-turn navigation and features tons of business listings. You can also search for various other items nearby, like ATMs and pharmacies. Finding a gas station or a restaurant while you're driving somewhere will work well enough that you won't have to switch apps.

Offline maps are available for many countries; you can go completely offline on your travels once you've downloaded the maps, which is helpful if you're going to cross a border and perhaps face higher data costs. It's also ideal to use for areas with patchy mobile coverage. While Google Maps' chatbot can find appointments and call to book them for you, Here WeGo has a simpler appeal. This isn't going to be the best app to use if you want to discover new places, but it will take you to your destination just fine — with fewer distractions.

TomTom

TomTom has been making GPS devices for decades, so naturally, its mobile app is a top contender as a Google Maps alternative for Android Auto. It's the same no-frills, distraction-free design, so you can focus on driving. If you find Google Maps too busy on your car's screen, TomTom's simpler interface might be enough reason to switch. You can also change your route if you need to and mark various issues like speed traps and closed roads. One of its better features is that when you choose a place you need to visit, the app lets you search for nearby parking. That's particularly handy when you're driving to a location you're unfamiliar with, so you don't have to go around the block a dozen times just to find available spots.

TomTom (formerly AmiGO) itself is free, but drivers who want more, like offline navigation, can pay for TomTom GO Expert. MapQuest

Hackers haven’t eased off this month after waging a massive crime spree in October, and are now targeting foundational institutions of Western power, including top national security agencies.

Last month, cyberattacks hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. Targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, and the State Bank of India. Cyberattacks even reached freezers across Europe and at U.S. military bases, with temperatures hiked high enough to spoil frozen food. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.”

Cybersecurity experts also rushed to fix vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language that’s used in nearly 70% of all websites. Black October reached a crescendo with the largest crypto heist in history: North Korean hackers swiped $6.3 billion from Binance.

But November has seen a new string of cyber incidents. Sources told Reuters on Friday that hackers broke into Cloud One, the U.S. Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform. The breach was discovered in the past month during upgrades to the system. It was unclear who was behind it, how far the intruders got, or whether any data was taken, the report said.

The attackers used a software vulnerability to reach the platform’s control plane, which is comparable to a universal remote, according to Reuters. In theory, access at that level could let intruders check the operational status of military aircraft or track the movement of spare parts.

“A breach here is a big deal,” a source told Reuters.

Cloud One was designed as a single home for the Air Force’s IT needs, running scores of applications — including a system that consolidates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America as well as a system that tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 Air Force locations worldwide.

Since the breach was discovered, efforts to move back-office applications onto Cloud One have been paused, while updates to applications already on the platform have been blocked, sources told Reuters.

Meanwhile, sources told the New York Times on Tuesday that the Central Intelligence Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information.

It affected an open-source intelligence analysis system and a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, the report added.

Earlier this month, CNN reported that hackers penetrated the FBI’s National Crime Information Center, marking the second such incident in recent months. A possible cyberattack also forced the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network to take some services offline.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon has been dealing with the fallout from a breach last year that exposed Social Security numbers, dates of birth and other military personnel information. Similarly, a leak dubbed “Icepick” exposed personnel records for Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors last month.

In Europe, FIFA said Thursday that hackers stole personal and business information from FIFA the global governing body for soccer. And the UK’s Department for Work and Pensions, which administers Britain’s welfare system, took many of its services offline on Friday as officials declined to rule out a cyberattack.

Companies weren’t spared wither. Travel-booking platform Expedia confirmed Thursday to Skift that hackers breached its systems via a third-party data provider.

Researchers say there is little evidence that ordinary hackers are using AI to exploit complex vulnerabilities. Instead, the technology is mostly being used to scale up phishing campaigns.

At the same time, AI models can find vulnerabilities far faster than humans, setting off a race in where defenders try to find and fix flaws before attackers exploit them.

In fact, the string of cyberattacks followed a series of network outages caused by companies rushing out security patches. On Nov. 12, Microsoft’s suite of software tools went offline, shutting down email and calendars as well as collaboration and AI functions.

Days later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. And the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network also went down.

The Trump administration has insisted that the surge in network outages isn’t due to a cyberattack, but those responsible for the federal government’s emergency response aren’t so sure.

Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.

One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.

“There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”

For would-be homebuyers hoping for a reprieve in mortgage rates next year, the outlook isn’t good as borrowing costs are expected to remain high.

According to Freddie Mac, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.21% as of Wednesday, down from last week’s average of 7.28% as the stock market selloff pushed investors to safe haven Treasuries, lowering bond yields. But at this same time last year, the 30-year rate was 6.23%.

The rate spike in recent months has frozen the housing market. Sales of existing homes plunged 5.5% in October from the prior month and 8.8% from a year ago to an annualized pace of just 3.75 million units, the lowest in 16 years. Pending sales, an indicator of future closings, hit a second consecutive record low in October, down 4.7% month over month and 16.7% year over year.

Americans are also physically stuck. The housing turnover rate, which is how often homes get new owners, is just 3.8% a year, well below the 5% rate before the financial crisis. And the rate at which people move from region to region has been falling for two years.

Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of this year and through mid-2027 with sales falling 3.5%, potentially dampening the spring selling season and weighing further on the housing market next year.

The problem is that inflation is accelerating, so the Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep hiking rates, which will push up borrowing costs across the economy.

To be sure, oil prices have eased as the Iran war continues to simmer without re-escalating, but the latest consumer price index came in hotter than expected with inflationary pressure spreading beyond energy categories.

Ironically, the frozen housing market is also stoking inflation, keeping the Fed hawkish, as discouraged buyers turn to the rental market and push up rents.

“New-lease rents are growing at their fastest pace in 2025-2026, so they’re no longer pulling down housing inflation measures, and forecasts for on-market rents have been revised upward in recent months,” Zillow Senior Economist Kara Ng wrote earlier this month. “In other words, while oil-related developments could ease some inflation pressure, firmer rent growth means the Fed may get less help from shelter in 2027.”

The U.S. economy is also booming as AI hyperscalers pour hundreds of billions of dollars into data centers and other infrastructure. Their capital expenditures are expected to top $1 trillion in 2027. Third-quarter GDP jumped 4.3%, and the fourth quarter is on pace to see still-robust growth of 2.9%.

That continues to support strong wages and resilient consumer demand, allowing businesses to pass on higher costs and add further to inflation.

“However, a slowdown elsewhere in the economy or faster progress on inflation would pull mortgage rates down sooner,” Ng pointed out. “With inventory forecast to rise about 11% next year, there should be enough supply to meet demand if buyers return.”

For now, the housing market is still reeling from the mortgage rate shock. The 30-year fixed mortgage had been around 6.60% in July, then soared to 7.61% by the start of October, and has stayed above 7% since then.

Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman told CNBC earlier this month that the full-percentage-point surge was one of the fastest three-month increases seen in decades. That has sent the purchase mortgage market down 4% year over year, and he expects it to be down 10%-15% in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, rents in the third quarter were up nearly 20%.

“That is buyers just not being able to afford the homes they were looking at,” Wacksman explained. “They were thinking about a mortgage and then they couldn’t pull the trigger, and so now they’re renting longer.”

Why it is here: Explains the internal dynamics of a tech company and its impact on AI safety, with useful vocabulary.

“Anthropic is an unusual company. Some might say weird—and in fact, many have,” Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s cofounder and president, joked from the stage at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square, just hours before the company’s blockbuster IPO earlier this month. In her speech, Amodei stressed that the company was not like other technology companies, largely because of its “safety-first” culture.

Anthropic has long positioned itself as the most responsible AI lab. The company had an AI safety team before it even had a product. Its founders and employees have been vocal about AI risk, and even its IPO prospectus warned investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

For this reason, over the majority of its five-year history, Anthropic has counted the community of people focused on AI safety—both technical researchers and policy experts—among its closest allies. But in the run-up to the company’s IPO, some prominent figures in that once-sympathetic field openly broke with the company and now see it as a threat instead of an ally.

“Anthropic is absolutely not the voice of the AI safety community,” said Steven Adler, a former OpenAI safety researcher who co-founded Guidelight AI Standards, which sets safety benchmarks for AI companies. “Many researchers I know believe that Anthropic is the most likely company to get everyone killed.”

These divisions were on full display the day Anthropic made its market debut. Outside the company’s headquarters in San Francisco, more than 100 protesters gathered to demand a ban on “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, a term for using AI systems to autonomously build yet more powerful AI. Among them was Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher who made headlines around the globe when he quit in September over safety concerns.

Inside the company, Anthropic has, at times, struggled to keep hold of its safety-conscious culture as it has grown, according to three former employees and two people familiar with the company who spoke to Fortune. From its origins as a group of researchers primarily concerned with AI safety, Anthropic’s headcount has swelled to more than 5,000 employees, and its market value closed its first day of trading at about $1.76 trillion. (Since then, it has slipped closer to a $1 trillion market cap.) Now some are questioning whether Anthropic’s safety-first culture can survive life as a public company, and whether the company has already betrayed its founding principles.

“Anthropic has sought to create a race to the top on safety: to show that it’s possible to build AI carefully and succeed commercially, and to make safety something on which AI companies compete,” an Anthropic spokesperson said. “We remain true to our vision to build AI systems that put safety and humans at the center, while maximizing the benefits for humanity.”

“A close second”

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, led by the siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. The group split off primarily because they felt OpenAI’s leadership was not taking AI safety seriously enough and was not trustworthy enough to control such a powerful technology, several former employees said. (Personal conflicts between OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei also played a role, some said.)

Because of that founding mission, most of the company’s early employees came from the AI safety community. Many also hailed from the world of effective altruism—a philanthropic movement that uses evidence and reason to try to do the most good and whose adherents came to rank AI as one of humanity’s most neglected risks. To this day, Anthropic has more people who are adherents of effective altruism, or share many of its values, than rival labs, two former employees who spoke to Fortune said.

Much of Anthropic’s early money also came from EA-aligned investors. Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn, who has backed a number of EA-affiliated organizations, led Anthropic’s $124 million Series A in May 2021, with Facebook cofounder Dustin Moskovitz, another major funder of EA-related philanthropies, and the Center for Emerging Risk Research also investing. A year later, Anthropic’s $580 million Series B was led by the disgraced crypto kingpin Sam Bankman-Fried, then the movement’s best-known donor.

In the early days, one of Anthropic’s principles was that it would not push the frontier of AI research, according to one former Anthropic engineer, who asked for anonymity to discuss sensitive information about their former employer. Leadership said explicitly that it did not want to start or worsen an AI arms race, and described the lab’s aim as being “a close second,” the person said. Most employees also believed strongly that advanced AI posed an existential risk to humanity.

The company continues to weigh safety concerns heavily, funds its safety teams generously, and holds onto its safety talent, former employees say. But some in Anthropic’s organization also have deep qualms about what the world looks like following the development of the kind of superintelligent AI Anthropic wants to build.

David Duvenaud, a University of Toronto professor who led Anthropic’s Alignment Evaluations team from 2023 to 2024, says many early Anthropic employees believed AI presented a chance of destroying or enslaving humanity. (Duvenaud himself has put the odds of AI destroying much of what humanity values at 70% to 80% by the year 2100).

As a result, Anthropic initially didn’t want to release a product, former employees said. In the summer of 2022, months before OpenAI debuted ChatGPT, launching the AI boom, Anthropic had developed a working chatbot but chose not to release it. Dario Amodei later called that incident a “one-time overhang.”

As Anthropic has grown, its commitment to some of these early principles seems to have eroded. In March 2024, Anthropic released Claude 3, which by some measures beat OpenAI’s GPT-4. It no longer seemed to be playing just for second place.…

Because no team claimed him off waivers on Thursday, Pittsburgh is obligated for the rest of that guarantee. A team that claimed him would have assumed the contract. None did, and NFL insiders Tom Pelissero and Dianna Russini both reported no immediate interest from other teams.

What Rodgers will be paid in 2026

If the guarantee holds, Rodgers will finish 2026 with about $22.5 million from Pittsburgh, up from the $13.65 million base value of his first Steelers contract a year earlier.

The deal could have reached $25 million. Insider Jordan Schultz reported $2.5 million in incentives that paid $625,000 for each Steelers playoff win, provided Rodgers played 75% of regular-season snaps. Those bonuses were tied to Pittsburgh’s postseason, which he is no longer part of.

He can still add to the total. If he signs elsewhere, it would likely be at the veteran minimum of about $75,000 a week, and the Steelers would remain responsible for the rest of his salary, sports litigator Jay Reisinger told Pittsburgh’s WTAE.

Can Pittsburgh get the money back?

Possibly, but not easily. The NFL’s collective bargaining agreement lets a club deny termination pay to a player released for conduct detrimental to the team, a call that ultimately goes to an arbitrator. ESPN reported that if the Steelers filed and won such a grievance, they would get the remaining $8.56 million back as a salary-cap credit after the season. Until then, his $22.5 million cap charge for 2026 is unaffected.

There is no indication yet that the team plans to try, Front Office Sports reported Friday, and the NFL Players Association would be expected to fight any attempt. Reisinger told WTAE the likelier outcome is a settlement “somewhere south of $7 million.”

Rodgers has offered his own account of the split. In a message read by Al Michaels during Amazon Prime Video’s Black Friday broadcast, he said the team went public first and added: “They also barred me from the facility. That’s why I went to McAfee.” Steelers owner Art Rooney II has said he has “100% confidence in Mike McCarthy.”

The fallout has reached the box office, too. Steelers ticket prices on the secondary market fell 36% in three days after the release, Front Office Sports reported.

A fortune built mostly on salary

Rodgers’ net worth has never been publicly disclosed. His documented pay is about $417 million in career NFL earnings including this season, according to Spotrac. That is nearly $400 million more than Mason Rudolph, the backup who replaced him and led Pittsburgh to a 27-5 win over Denver on Friday.

Endorsements add to his assets. Rodgers left Nike for a multiyear deal with Adidas in 2015, as Fortune reported at the time, and Forbes estimated his 2022 earnings at $68 million, including $11 million off the field.

Rodgers turns 43 on Dec. 2. In May, he said 2026 would be his final NFL season. If no team calls, his last check from the league will come from a franchise that no longer wants him around, and may yet try not to send it.

The investor Lauren C. Templeton is not a pessimist—though she’s happiest when everyone around her is.

The Tennessee-based author and fund manager has taken up the creed of “maximum pessimism” espoused by her legendary great-uncle, Sir John Templeton, whom many view as the greatest stock picker of the 20th century. Sir John famously said that every bull market is born in pessimism, which creates an environment where bargains abound—if you know where to look for them.

Templeton, who began her career working alongside her renowned great-uncle, has likewise made a name for herself by placing bets in bad times. Those bets have included buying airline stocks after 9/11 and scooping up Amazon shares at the outset of the pandemic. She and her husband run the hedge fund Templeton and Phillips Capital Management, with $325 million in assets.

Templeton inherited her contrarian investment style from her great-uncle, but also from her stockbroker father. She recalls the time he returned home from work on Black Monday in 1987—a day when the Dow Jones plunged 23%—and told her mother he was the only broker in his branch to put in a buy order.

As a child, Templeton says, she was passionate about stocks because purchasing even a single share made her feel like a part owner of the company. She once even wrote a letter of disappointment to Walmart founder Sam Walton about a filthy restroom she encountered at a store. (Walton wrote back promising to tighten things up.)

Today, Templeton’s investment thesis reflects Warren Buffett’s famous maxim to “be greedy when others are fearful.” It’s a sound strategy, but that doesn’t mean it’s easy. Here are three rules she follows.

1. Know how to play the waiting game

“There are only three sources of alpha available in the markets: You can have a better model; you can have better information; or you can have better behavior,” says Templeton.

“Behavior” in this case means discipline, which can be hard to maintain in times of volatility. The undoing of many retail investors, says Templeton, comes from selling when the market is diving—a decision that can lead to unloading good assets and, even worse, missing out on the big bounce backs that often follow selloffs. Indeed, there is sobering research that shows that, over the past 30 years, 78% of the stock market’s best days occurred during bear markets and in the first two months of a bull market—and that missing the market’s 10 best days during that period would have reduced your portfolio by half.

Templeton stresses that it’s crucial for investors to know how to wait. She says her fund’s approach can be unsettling for younger employees, who may be itching to trade. “I always tell them, ‘We’re just sitting around reading. It’s not going to be an eventful day-to-day environment, because we don’t overtrade.’”

This premium on patience is something Templeton also conveys to potential investors. While they may appreciate her “maximum pessimism” philosophy, not all have the stomach for it. “If clients hire and fire managers based on their own personal cycles of fear and greed, the strategy breaks,” she says. “A major part of our responsibility isn’t just managing the asset allocation, but actively managing our investors’ emotions.”

2. Keep a wish list at the ready

The investing success of Sir John Templeton, who as a student at Yale paid for his tuition in part by playing poker, was based on a clever trick of psychology: He kept a wish list of stocks at the ready for the next downturn, which helped anchor his thinking when opportunity arose. His grandniece uses the same strategy.

“The psychological pressure of a market crash is immense. When prices tank, human nature forces you to obsess over your losses and fear opening your financial statements,” she says. “But if you can actively shift your mindset by pulling out a preapproved list of elite companies that you’ve always wanted to own but found too expensive, the script completely flips. Suddenly, a market crash becomes an exciting shopping spree.”

She and her partner and spouse, Scott Phillips, use this strategy not only to buy quality stocks on the cheap when the market dives, but also to turn their portfolio over. To do this, they typically use a dollar-cost averaging approach to take large positions in new stocks while divesting other ones they hold.

The couple employed this strategy during the financial crisis of late 2008 and early 2009. Templeton recalls this period, which brought about the collapse of numerous major banks, with happy nostalgia. “At that point, asset prices were so detached from reality that it felt like shooting fish in a barrel,” she says.

3. There’s always a bargain—somewhere in the world

It’s easy enough to understand the idea of waiting to buy at the bottom of the market. The problem, of course, is that no one—including Templeton—can be sure exactly when the bottom is in.

“The simple answer is that you don’t ever truly know,” she says. “We might be getting a little uncomfortable or excited as prices plummet, but we don’t have a crystal ball. You simply observe that a massive cluster of high-quality bargains has emerged, and you want to get your hands on them.”

Such moments don’t come along all the time. Indeed, the current bull market in U.S. equities recently entered its fifth year. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t opportunities to find elsewhere.

Templeton recalls that her great-uncle realized this in the late 1950s and 1960s when he looked at publicly traded companies in Japan. He understood that investors had significantly undervalued these firms because of lingering anti-Japanese sentiment from World War II as well as quirks in the companies’ accounting that didn’t properly account for subsidiary profits. Sir John bought shares—and profited handsomely.…

Deep in the Alaka‘i plateau, 4,000 feet high in the mountains of the remote Hawaiian island of Kaua‘i, the forest is quiet.

For conservationists at the Kaua‘i Forest Bird Recovery Project, this silence is both a somber reminder of species already lost, as well as an eerie omen of what’s to come. Last year, Kaua‘i lost its last wild ‘akikiki, a tiny gray forest bird found nowhere else on Earth. After having evolved over millions of years deep in the forests of Kaua‘i, now only a few dozen ʻakikiki exist in captive breeding centers on O‘ahu and Hawai‘i Island.

That same fate befell the small greenish-yellow ‘akekeke, whose wild population wildlife biologists estimate is down to a handful. Populations of the once-abundant olive-green Kaua‘i ‘amakihi have plummeted, from around 9,000 birds in 2023, when the last survey was conducted, to under 500 by conservationists’ estimates this year. Even the ‘anianiau, the lemon yellow, “mouse-like” honeycreeper last thought by wildlife biologists to have more than 3,000 individuals in the wild in 2023, is down to only a few hundred.

In June, researchers announced a stark estimate to a group of Kaua‘i’s local lawmakers: Every one of Kaua‘i’s endemic honeycreeper species could be lost as soon as Christmas.

“Numbers we’d previously estimated in the hundreds, we’re not seeing at all,” said Lisa “Cali” Crampton of the Kaua‘i Forest Bird Recovery Project.

An “Explosion” of Mosquitoes Drives Decline of Birds

The sudden drop in native bird populations comes after an unprecedented mosquito swarm took hold in Kaua‘i’s higher-elevation forests, taking both scientists and conservationists by surprise, Crampton said. These southern house mosquitoes are responsible for spreading avian malaria, a disease that can prove fatal to honeycreepers after only one or two bites.

Narrowing down an exact number of honeycreepers left in the wild has been no easy task for Crampton and her team, who travel deep into the Alaka‘i swamp—a dense, wet forest located over 4,000 feet above sea level. The crew must traverse thick, remote woods and wetland bogs for days at a time to even glimpse the tiny birds.

Considering how fast her team has witnessed the mosquitoes spreading, Crampton fears the researchers’ population estimates from their last official survey in 2023 are wildly out of date. Even amid the wrath of catastrophic hurricanes—most recently Hurricane Lowell, which struck Kaua‘i on September 7th—conservationists struggle to imagine a greater threat to the birds than the mosquito swarms.

“I was hugely worried about a giant hurricane just like Lowell coming and having a direct hit on the island and wiping out a bunch of our birds,” said Justin Hite, mosquito project coordinator for the Hawai‘i Division of Forestry and Wildlife. “However, in some ways I’m less worried now. Because the mosquito storm that hit us last winter, that was already way more devastating than a hurricane really could ever be.”

In fall 2025, field workers noticed that mosquitoes were deeper in the forest than ever before.

“We went from one mosquito per trap per night, maybe three or maybe four mosquitoes per trap per night on a bad night, to 300 mosquitoes per trap per night in the span of two months,” Crampton recalled.

The sudden “explosion” of mosquitoes left conservation workers scrambling for an explanation, and worried that their efforts to eradicate the insects with a combination of natural bacteria-based insecticides and the release of sterile male mosquitoes—what’s known as incompatible insect technique—might be futile in the face of such a dramatic bloodsucker boom.

Kaua‘i’s endemic honeycreepers also serve as the proverbial canary in a coal mine, Crampton explained, warning of what’s to come for other higher-elevation forests across the Hawaiian archipelago. For honeycreeper conservationists, it’s now a race against time to prepare the islands’ birds before the inevitable spread of the mosquitoes across all of Hawai‘i’s high-elevation forests.

More Than a Perfect Storm

There are several environmental factors that affect mosquito populations, from precipitation levels to wind patterns, said Jeff Foster, professor of biological sciences at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff, Arizona. But ultimately, he said, they all boil down to one main cause: rising temperatures from global climate change.

Increasing temperatures across the Hawaiian Islands over the last several years have pushed mosquitoes farther up into higher elevations, Foster said. And a trick of topography left the birds of Kaua‘i, which only rises to about 5,000 feet and lacks the high-elevation forests of taller islands like Hawai‘i and Maui, without habitat high enough to escape the pests.

Surprisingly, drier conditions in Kaua‘i’s forests also provide better habitat for mosquitoes, Foster said. “We would typically assume that with more precipitation that we would get more mosquitoes,” Foster explained. “And in lots of places that’s true, but it’s not true with our experience in Hawai‘i.”

Additionally, as Kaua‘i’s mountains are shaped like plateaus rather than steadily inclining peaks, the island did not have many birds living in the steep “transition zone” between low-elevation and high-elevation forests. This meant that conservationists were not able to observe the steady decline in bird populations in this middle-elevation forest, Foster explained. The mosquito boom, he said, only seems sudden because scientists couldn’t accurately track the mosquito’s progression.

“We knew it was coming, but we thought we had more time,” said Foster. “And then suddenly we didn’t have any more time and it’s worse than we imagined.”

Avian malaria is incredibly common, Foster noted. Anywhere between 18 percent and 35 percent of birds globally carry the disease, but it rarely causes mass mortality events.

So why is it so deadly to Kaua‘i’s honeycreepers?…

Surveying the wreckage in the weeks after the Camp Fire — tens of thousands of people displaced, 85 percent of the town’s buildings destroyed and all but one campus of Paradise Unified School District damaged — it was hard for Jake Timm to imagine when or if the town’s population might recover. It could be 15 or 20 years before enough students returned to fill the schools in the Northern California community, thought Timm, the district’s director of facilities, maintenance and operations.

“I don’t think we knew exactly what we were stepping into,” said Timm. “Especially when we got up here after the fire to assess the damage, when part of the town was still smoldering.”

But after falling precipitously in the years after the 2018 wildfire, California’s deadliest on record, the district’s enrollment began to rebound. Today, it’s up to 1,817 students — still just 53 percent of enrollment pre-fire but enough for the district to speed up the timeline for rebuilding its second elementary school in Paradise to meet demand. This fall the school became the last of the district’s campuses to reopen post-fire, and there are already plans to add new classrooms. An average of just over 80 new students arrive each year.

School districts across the country are dealing with sharp enrollment declines brought about primarily because of falling birthrates, and California’s drop is among the most pronounced. But in Paradise, district officials are seeing an unexpected increase in younger students, as more young families relocate to the area, drawn by its relative affordability and new development.

Still, even as Paradise Unified School District completes the physical rebuilding process, lingering effects on academics show the long tail of post-disaster recovery.

Over a quarter of Paradise Unified’s students are chronically absent, a rate that’s more than 10 percentage points higher than the state average. Graduation rates and state test scores have also suffered.

That aligns with the growing body of research on the impact of wildfires and other disasters on education. In the short term, disasters and extreme weather can lead to increased absences and adverse learning outcomes. Longer term, research has linked experiencing a natural disaster to fewer years of total schooling completed, which in turn can correlate to reduced higher education outcomes and potential lifetime earnings.

And recovering from wildfires and other disasters is becoming an increasingly common challenge for school districts in California and elsewhere, as climate change drives more frequent extreme weather events and more severe disasters. Approximately 25 percent of public schools in the U.S. are located in census tracts designated as very high risk from at least one environmental hazard, including coastal flooding, hurricanes, heat waves, and wildfires, according to research from Brown University’s SustainableED initiative. In the coming years, more of them will face difficult questions about if, and how, to rebuild.

When Southern California’s Pasadena Unified School District — which faced declining enrollment for over a decade before the January 2025 Eaton Fire destroyed more than 9,000 buildings — weighed consolidating its schools earlier this year, families were outraged. Students who lost their homes in the fire said their still-standing schools offered stability and community; in a local editorial, one parent questioned why the district would consider closing schools so soon after the fire, when rebuilding might draw more families.

And after the 110-year-old King Kamehameha III Elementary School was destroyed in the August 2023 Maui wildfires, the majority of community members wanted the historic campus rebuilt in the same location. But state education officials said the campus couldn’t be rebuilt there because of limited space, flood risk and other factors, and instead chose a different site about a half-mile away and outside of the tsunami inundation zone.

Near Paradise, the tiny Golden Feather Union Elementary School District was also affected by the Camp Fire. The water system at the district’s only school, Concow Elementary, was severely damaged, and overall recovery in the more rural and lower-income community of Concow has been slower than in Paradise. The district relocated students to an elementary campus it had closed back in 2010, where they remain today. The new site is about 8 miles from Concow Elementary and closer to the town of Oroville, where many families relocated.

Only two Paradise Unified schools reopened in their original locations shortly after the fire: Pine Ridge Elementary and Cedarwood Elementary, both located in Magalia, which is just northeast of Paradise. Students from other schools spent the months after the fire scattered across Butte County. The junior high operated out of a hardware store, while the two high schools moved to independent study with drop-in hours at a mall. Paradise Elementary and Ponderosa Elementary, which was also destroyed in the fire, both used classrooms provided by other districts, each 20 miles away from Paradise.

Among the town’s boosters, whether Paradise would rebuild wasn’t really a question. The city started on a long-term recovery plan right after the fire and set goals of making the community more fire-resilient and welcoming to new and returning residents.

“My son was a freshman in high school here in town when this all happened, and he said, ‘I won’t go anywhere but Paradise,’” said Timm. “We’re a very strong-headed community, the ones of us that are left here.”

Two days before the fire, residents had passed a $61 million bond to modernize schools and complete a list of maintenance projects. “We passed the bond, we were all, ‘Woo-hoo,’ and then we’re all evacuating,” said Timm.…

From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood with author David Helvarg.

Kelp forests are one of the most productive ecosystems on Earth, and the nearly 1 million square miles of them along the colder coastlines of the world are increasingly under threat from climate change.

Kelp’s vulnerability to changing ocean temperatures was barely mentioned at the 2026 “blue COP” in Turkey, and it’s only recently that these giant algae have even been given a place of importance in ocean conservation next to mangroves and coral reefs.

But kelp fronds pull a lot of carbon out of the sea and give back a fifth of the Earth’s oxygen. That’s as much as all of our rainforests combined.

In other words, kelp forests are the “Amazon of the ocean,” as David Helvarg argues in his latest book, “Forest of the Sea: The Remarkable Life and Imperiled Future of Kelp.” And like the Amazon, as the planet warms, kelp forests suffer—not from flames, but from marine heat waves and pollution.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

STEVE CURWOOD: Reading your book, one of the takeaways is: Look, there’s so much going wrong with the ecosystem based on what we’ve done to the climate, and people feel a little helpless. But one possible inflection point is to deal with kelp because we still have a lot of it, comparatively speaking, and it will make a huge difference for dealing with a climate emergency. To what extent is that statement true?

DAVID HELVARG: It’s very true. Unfortunately, unlike coral reefs or rainforests, people know very little about the world’s kelp forests, which actually cover more territory than the Amazon—up to almost a third of the coastlines of the world. Along with estuaries and salt marshes, mangroves and seagrasses, they generate 20 percent of the oxygen. They have a tremendous amount because they’re an algae that photosynthesizes; they absorb huge amounts of carbon dioxide in the water.

Unlike farmland, which often results in deforestation and also needs all these inputs like fossil fuel-based herbicides and fertilizers, kelp and seaweeds get their nutrients out of the water and produce very high-value foods. Most people still think that seafood is mostly wild-caught. Today, it’s 140 million tons of agricultural product a year versus 90 million tons of wild-caught species; of that 140 million, 30 million tons a year is seaweeds, including kelps and other high-nutrient-value crops.

CURWOOD: Given that kelp forests are so large and so vital, why do you suppose most people don’t know about them? They seem to be unknown to the general public.

HELVARG: They’re just offshore, but they’re offshore in colder waters where tourists don’t go. People walking the beach, they may see the canopy offshore, but mostly they just see it as piles of smelly kelp that’s washed up and covered with flies. Most people don’t realize that kelp is 40 percent alginate, which is a great stabilizer and emulsifier. So that kelp product is in all our processed foods, in our toothpaste, our cosmetics.

CURWOOD: Ice cream too, right?

HELVARG: Ice cream, too. It makes it more creamy and less icy. We wouldn’t have chicken nuggets without alginate. It’s also in medicines, like antacid capsules. It’s worth $500 billion a year, and yet, few people know it’s there.

CURWOOD: Let’s go into the science of this. I’ve seen some kelp forests. There’s some wonderful ones in Monterey Bay and also off of South Africa, Cape Town. They look like trees, but in fact, they are something else—some sort of super algae.

HELVARG: It’s what they call evolutionary convergence. The kelp forests look a lot like plants, but they’re actually really big algae, like the giant kelp we have here in California, and the bull kelp. Literally, they’re the bamboo of the ocean. They can grow a foot, two feet a day.

Algae gave birth to the plant system. The first complex life on Earth was 1.2 billion years ago when different algae formed, and eventually that led to the plant systems on land. And 600 million years later, the animal kingdom rose up. When we say the forest of the sea, we scientifically have to point out it’s algae, not plants.

CURWOOD: Tell me what the kelp do in the ecosystem. What organisms, aside from themselves, of course, do they nurture?

HELVARG: Aside from providing protection from erosion and storm impacts and providing oxygen, they protect over 1,000 species, like leafy sea dragons and wolf eels. The life cycles of a lot of our edible wildlife, like salmon and cod and herring, also depend on the kelp forest, where they mature and spend a year or more breeding. Herring roe on kelp is one of the first foods of spring for Indigenous communities all along the Pacific Coast. Commercial fishers around the world are very dependent on it, and other people are dependent on it as a harvest. In Asia there are huge amounts of kelp harvesting for food and other products.

CURWOOD: You’re both a journalist and a scuba diver. What was it like to experience these forests for the first time?

HELVARG: Well, it’s kind of amazing. Even if it wasn’t producing $500 billion in a year in goods and services, it’s just inherently one of those places with a sense of awe and wonder that you’re part of something mysterious. It’s fun to dive in coral, but kelp diving is a full-contact sport. You’re going through these thick and tangling kelp, and it’s dark and it’s murky. Suddenly the light will break through, like somebody fired a shotgun through a barn door. You had these intense shafts of light that were lighting up the world around us, which is a world of giant Garibaldis. They’re like goldfish on steroids. Then you look down, and there’s a wolf eel—big gray teeth and snaggletoothed—just so ugly it’s attractive.…

item.title: Will my glacier go extinct? Interview with Lander Van Tricht
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Educational interview with a researcher on glacier extinction, providing valuable information with moderate complexity.

- The Global Glacier Extinction Explorer is a platform that maps the world’s glaciers and projects when they’ll disappear under various global warming scenarios.

- The findings are bleak: even under the best-case scenario, “we will lose half of the glaciers on Earth,” says map developer Lander Van Tricht.

- Van Tricht and his colleagues developed the tool to help make science accessible to the general public and to provide information to communities that live in close proximity to glaciers.

In mid-October, Lander Van Tricht received a message from a woman. She had visited a glacier when she was 10 years old and, according to a tool that Van Tricht had developed, that same glacier was now expected to go extinct in less than 40 years.

Instances of public engagement like these were exactly what Van Tricht says he wished for while developing the tool. “What I really hoped was that scientific results are shared beyond the academic world,” Van Tricht, a postdoctoral researcher at ETH Zürich and Vrije Universiteit in Brussels, told Mongabay in a video interview.

The Global Glacier Extinction Explorer is an interactive platform that allows people to zoom in on glaciers on a map and find out how they’re faring in the face of global warming. The tool is based on the findings from a 2026 study, published in the journal Nature, that looked at the disappearance of individual glaciers.

The findings from the study, on which Van Tricht was the lead author, are dire. They show that even in a world where warming is limited to 1.5° Celsius (2.7° Fahrenheit) above the pre-industrial baseline, half of Earth’s glaciers will be lost. “I was surprised by how fast everything is happening,” Van Tricht says.

He adds he hopes the tool will help translate the science to the general public, and also help communities around the world prepare for scenarios where glaciers go extinct.

“Communities, cities and people have to prepare themselves for a future without glaciers, he says. “For them, it’s super important to know how long a glacier they rely on will still be there.”

Lander Van Tricht spoke with Mongabay’s Abhishyant Kidangoor about the motivation behind building the Global Glacier Extinction Explorer, the findings that left him surprised, and what he hopes will come out of the tool. The following interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Mongabay: How would you describe the Global Glacier Extinction Explorer to someone who hasn’t heard about it before?

Lander Van Tricht: We know glaciers are losing mass. They’re getting smaller, and many of them are just disappearing. They’re becoming too small and we don’t consider those as glaciers anymore, but as extinct glaciers. The Global Glacier Extinction Explorer allows people to zoom in into every individual glacier on Earth, click on it, and see when it will disappear or if it will survive beyond the end of the century.

Mongabay: What’s the backstory behind this tool? What was your motivation behind doing this?

Lander Van Tricht: In scientific research, we typically publish in journals. By doing this, we try to reach an audience and get our main results into climate reports. That’s always what we hope for. But it’s very difficult to really reach [a] general audience. My colleagues and I had a feeling that we have to try to put more effort into reaching everyone. For this, we needed to think about visualization and ways to communicate.

The goal of this tool was really to translate the scientific findings into an easy, accessible format where everyone can really go and find out the results.

Mongabay: Why is doing this more important now than ever before?

Lander Van Tricht: People are witnessing the impacts of climate change on glaciers. If you’re in the mountains and you see a glacier today and you know how it was before, you’re really confronted by these changes.

For a general audience, it’s important to know about these changes. How fast are they happening? When will a glacier disappear? On the other hand, communities, cities and people have to prepare themselves for a future without glaciers. For them, it’s super important to know how long a glacier they rely on will still be there.

Imagine a valley with one glacier, which is very important as a tourism attractor. Do they need to have investments in tourism infrastructure, or is it not worth it because the glacier will disappear in five years? This community can look up the results and see how long the glacier will be there. Same for ski resorts. Do they need to invest in ski infrastructure, or is it not worth it?

On the other hand, for people that rely on glacier runoff and water provided by glaciers, they need to know long this will be possible or when the glacier will disappear and not provide water anymore. So it’s really for communities, cities and countries to use the results to prepare for the future.

Mongabay: The tool is based on a recent study of yours. If you were to highlight the findings from the study, how would you do it?

Lander Van Tricht: One big highlight is that even in a 1.5° warming scenario, which is very positive, we will lose half of the glaciers on Earth. This is a huge number and, in fact, the decision on losing these glaciers is already made. We cannot do anything about them anymore.

In many mountain ranges with small glaciers, like the Alps and Caucasus, even in a 2.7°[C, or 4.9°F] scenario, which is the scenario where we seem to head to, almost all glaciers disappear in these mountain ranges. So there is almost no future anymore for glaciers in these mountain ranges because they are very sensitive. The loss trajectory has already started. These mountain ranges will just completely “de-glacierize” in any case.…

I wanted something economically feasible with all the fatty goodness of beef. So I took a page from Chinese take-out spots and opted for chuck, which is meaty and delicious but has lots of connective tissue. After a little bit of butchering and then coating the slices of beef in cornstarch and baking soda before stir-frying (a technique called velveting), you get the best of all worlds: a consistently tender, beefy bite. Usually this dish comes with water spinach, but I went with A-choy for sweet freshness, though my craziest addition is butter. It’s not a lot, but it gives the sacha beef an inexplicable depth. Just go with it.

I have been teaching a graduate seminar on Orientalism and representation at MIT for the last 34 years. Centered around Edward Said’s 1978 book Orientalism, the course examines the ways fraught relationships between the “West” and the “Orient” have been represented across different media since at least the Renaissance. Every two years, as I prepare to teach the seminar anew, I ask myself whether it might be time to shelve the subject, which has become so mainstream and seemingly overanalyzed. And every two years, something happens on the world stage that convinces me it’s still necessary.

This year, in addition to the rising racism against Muslims and Arabs in European and American political discourse; the vilification of Palestinians, Yemenis, and Iranians in Western media as their homelands are being destroyed; the suppression of Muslim rights in Modi’s India; and the continuing erasure of Muslim identities in Myanmar and China, an exhibition enigmatically titled “Orientalism: Between Fact and Fantasy” has reaffirmed the urgency of Said’s critique of Orientalism as a “Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient.” I will be teaching the seminar again next fall.

The exhibition, on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York until February 28, is the latest in a succession of exhibitions devoted to Orientalist art mounted around the world over the past three decades. As such, it introduces little material that has not already appeared in similar contexts, highlighting celebrated 19th-century Orientalist painters, principally Jean-Léon Gérôme (1824–1904) and Osman Hamdi Bey (1842–1910), among orientalizing 19th-century vases, plates, lamps, and ewers; old photos of “Orientals” and the Orient; and a number of representations of bashi-bozouks, the general term Europeans used to designate the unruly and reckless irregulars in Oriental armies.

Yet, to my mind, its most ingenious maneuver is the way it manages to circumvent nearly half a century of sustained criticism of Orientalism without openly challenging that criticism. Indeed, it even enshrines the first hardcover edition of Said’s Orientalism, with its famous cover reproducing Gérôme’s The Snake Charmer (1879), as a fetish object in a glass case alongside three Turkish helmets without incorporating its arguments into its texts. The rest of that gallery is largely devoted to dissecting Gérôme’s controversial painting, explaining where the artist might have found his visual sources.

A TELLING OMMISSION transpires at the entrance connecting the museum’s Islamic galleries to the Orientalist exhibition, where the arrangement, to my eyes, suggests considerably more than the wall text explicitly states. Two glass cases flank the opening. On the left is a copy of Pascal Coste’s Architecture arabe: ou, Monuments du Kaire, mesurés et dessinés, de 1818 à 1826 (1837–39); on the right, a volume of the monumental Description de l’Égypte, the multivolume encyclopedic survey (published between 1809 and 1829) that was produced by the army of scholars and scientists who accompanied Napoleon’s ill-fated invasion of Egypt (1798–1801). Together, the volumes invoke one of the exhibition’s principal themes: In the 19th century, Orientalism produced knowledge. Yet the critique—“knowledge is power”—on which Said, following Michel Foucault, insisted, goes unmentioned.

Meanwhile, the two paintings hanging above the cases make that power relationship unmistakable to the attentive viewer. Painted by Gérôme more than 60 years after the failure of the invasion and more than 40 years after Napoleon’s death, they belong to a series of hagiographic representations of Bonaparte in Egypt. One depicts Napoleon on horseback surveying Cairo, the city he conquered, from the ramparts of its Citadel. The other shows him defiantly confronting the Sphinx. Taken together, the paintings proclaim French dominion over Egypt’s present and past, precisely the ambition underlying Napoleon’s first colonial venture into the Orient.

That they were painted around the time of the contentious renegotiations between Ismaʿil Pasha, Egypt’s ruler (1863–79), and the French-dominated Suez Canal Company, headed by Ferdinand de Lesseps (1805–94), may be more than coincidental. Those negotiations culminated in an inequitable compensation settlement imposed on Egypt through the arbitration of Napoleon III, who regarded the canal as a prestige project for the Second French Empire. Gérôme’s resurrection of Napoleon I’s Egyptian campaign, at a moment when France was consolidating its economic and political influence over Egypt, had a charge that would hardly have escaped his contemporaneous French audience. None of this historical context, however, is mentioned in the exhibition.

If France’s imperial ambitions in Egypt were primarily financial and economic exploitation, its colonization of Algeria was considerably more direct and brutal. Following the invasion of 1830, French armies spent decades attempting to suppress Algerian resistance, most prominently that led by Emir ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jazāʾirī, represented here in a melancholy photographic portrait taken in 1860 by the Parisian firm Mayer & Pierson. The caption cryptically states that he “was the spiritual and military leader of Algeria following the French invasion of the country in 1830” and that “hoping to end his people’s suffering, he surrendered in 1847, living as a prisoner in France.”

What precisely was the emir doing as a leader? Who was responsible for his people’s suffering? What circumstances compelled him to surrender, and why was he subsequently imprisoned? The caption hints at these questions without answering them, leaving me wondering how a visitor unfamiliar with the history of French colonialism could possibly make sense of such evasive formulations, which transform a protracted struggle against conquest into an almost inexplicable sequence of personal decisions and misfortunes.…

Timber grid and external stair offer “a wink” to Centre Pompidou at its annexe in Massy

French architecture studio PCA-Stream has completed Centre Pompidou Francilien in Massy, a storage and exhibition space fronted by a gridded timber deck and external stair that echo the high-tech character of the iconic original Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Officially named Centre Pompidou Francilien Fabrique de l’Art (Art Factory), the 30,000-square-metre building is the first Centre Pompidou annexe in Île-de-France. It is scheduled to open to the public in spring 2027.

Overlooking a small lake, the building will house over 150,000 pieces from the Centre Pompidou’s reserve collections made visible to the public through temporary exhibition spaces, alongside private conservation and restoration areas.

It was built around a nine-metre cubic grid described by the studio as “a giant Sol LeWitt” artwork, which creates open, flexible spaces for both storage and exhibitions.

The grid is fronted by an open timber frame and traversed via an external staircase dubbed “the caterpillar”, nodding to the glass-tube escalators at the original Pompidou Centre in Beaubourg, Paris.

“The brief posed a paradoxical question: how do you display what normally remains invisible?” PCA-Stream founder Philippe Chiambretta told Dezeen.

“What truly constitutes the spirit of Beaubourg is not its image but its principle: large, flexible floor plates, made possible by great constructive rationality, which leave the institution free to reinvent its uses over time. That is the heritage we wanted to carry into Massy,” he added.

“The caterpillar, by contrast, is a gesture in the literal sense: a wink, a homage. The great timber stair that climbs the facade quotes the escalator on the outside of the Paris building, like a label of the Beaubourg spirit.”

Across the grid is a shifting gradient of openness, which moves from the more enclosed storage and restoration areas in the centre and eastern half of the building, where the facade is finished with curved metal louvres that control the entry of natural light.

The open timber stair on the western side of the centre connects a cafe and book store on the ground floor to the exhibitions level in the centre of the building and a rooftop terrace above.

“Beaubourg had pioneered the idea of a museum open to the city, with its piazza and its urban, accessible ambience. In Massy, we transposed this generosity of spirit into a different setting, no longer the dense urban fabric of Paris but a landscape of park, lake and trees,” said Chiambretta.

“Visitors never enter the vault, but they experience the whole building as a sequence that leads them from the water up to the canopy,” he added.

Behind the timber grid, the rest of the centre’s exterior has been finished with precast concrete panels, while inside the exhibition spaces sit beneath ceilings covered in black steel rigging.

Several museums in Europe have recently explored combining storage and display, giving visitors varying degrees of access behind-the-scenes. In London, Diller Scofidio + Renfro designed the V&A East Storehouse, while in 2021, MVRDV completed the Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen.

The Centre Pompidou is currently closed for five years as part of a renovation project being led by French studio Moreau Kusunoki Architectes and Mexican practice Frida Escobedo Studio.

Elastic Architects designs “theatrical” penthouse suites for Delano Miami Beach

At the newly reopened Delano Miami Beach, global firm Elastic Architects designed the hotel‘s penthouse interiors to further elevate the “cinematic” approach taken to renovating the art deco icon.

The property began welcoming guests back in June 2026 after a six-year, $100 million overhaul, which involved a historic restoration of the art deco building by Studio Mc+G Architecture and a full interior refresh by Elastic Architects.

Located on the Collins Avenue strip, the hotel was originally designed by architect B Robert Swartburg and opened in 1948. It was famously given a dazzling all-white interior by designer Philippe Starck in 1995.

Now operated by Ennismore, Delano Miami Beach has been brought up to date by a team that understood the hotel’s cultural significance and aimed to reclaim its icon status.

“It was a project that lived in the hearts of people for so many years and involved so many experiences,” Elastic Architects founder Ria Xenou told Dezeen.

“In very simple words, what was cool then is different from what is cool today.”

Her studio custom-designed every piece inside the hotel, from curvaceous seating and plush carpets to lighting and accessories at a range of scales to suit both soaring communal areas and cosy nooks.

“Delano was very cinematic – not so much about the specific pieces, as it was for the feel,” Xenou said.

The top-floor penthouses include Ocean View and City View suites, both designed to capture the essence of the historic hotel with a slightly more mellow, wellness-focused slant.

“The Delano penthouse used to be all about the party culture, but today we reimagined it around the luxury of taking care of oneself,” Xenou said.

While retaining a similar design scheme to the other 169 rooms and poolside bungalows, these expansive suites called for an even more bespoke design.

“The penthouse is a much more elevated, sophisticated, very high-end approach across every single element,” Xenou said.

“The brief was to design everything specifically for the location it’s being placed, and if you were to remove it, it doesn’t work. That’s the hardest brief we’ve ever gotten for a project.”

Each main penthouse has two bedrooms, but can be connected to smaller adjoining suites for larger groups or families.

Open-plan living and dining areas for entertaining connect to balconies, allowing guests to bring the party outside during Miami’s balmy nights.

Warm cream tones envelop the spaces, which are filled with curvy, soft-textured furniture and organic coves across the ceilings to evoke the waves and clouds outside.

The seating areas are oriented towards views, enabling guests to enjoy morning coffee overlooking the beach, or a cocktail while watching the sunset.

Huge mirrors in the bedrooms hide the TVs and also reflect the blue of the sea and sky visible through large sliding glass doors.

“It all speaks the same language of connecting the inside with the outside,” said Xenou.

The neutral-toned decor is accented by Calacatta Viola stone in the bathrooms and kitchen, while red lacquered-wood bedside tables tie the suites to the reimagined Rose Bar off the lobby downstairs.

“That’s our peekaboo moment,” said Xenou.

Artworks were also commissioned for the spaces from artists including Jerónimo Villa and Alejandra Aristizábal, who used a colour palette of sand, sky and coral hues to ensure the pieces blend in with the location.

A huge roof terrace that used to be part the hotel’s spa – now relocated to the basement – is set up as a private lounging area for guests with panoramic views of both ocean and city.

Penthouse occupants also have access to a new outdoor swimming pool reserved for Delano members and guests on the fourth floor, which is oriented to feel like a continuation of the original palm-fringed pool downstairs.

“There is this beautiful discussion and collaboration between the past and the present,” said Xenou of the two complementary areas.

The hotel has two restaurants: all-day Italian spot Gigi’s, which spills from the back of the hotel across an expansive covered terrace and out to the pool area, and Japanese eatery Mimi Kakushi upstairs.

A grab-and-go cafe at the front of the terrazzo-floored lobby sits below an ethereal ceiling-suspended light sculpture, and a custom pool table towards the back is positioned below a giant voluminous pendant lamp.

“All of that has been designed to feel out of proportion, a little bit magical,” Xenou said. “Maybe it feels like you’re under the sea, a little bit theatrical and cinematic.”

Excellent examples of the art deco style – which celebrated its centenary in 2025 – can be found all over Miami Beach, including the Pelican Hotel that was updated by Andrea Rosso last year.

The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds: Margaret Wise Brown’s Lost Masterpiece about Mortality and the Meaning of Life, Newly Illustrated

In early September 1948, a year after she rewilded the landscape of literature with Goodnight Moon, Margaret Wise Brown watched the love of her life fade to black.

Michael Strange, born Blanche Oelrichs, had cast an instant spell on Margaret — outspoken, sophisticated, and self-possessed, so tall Margaret had to lift her grey-blue eyes to meet the black of Michael’s, her tall frame clad in masculine clothing she herself had designed to cling to her curves, with a musical voice unspooling from her haunting dark beauty, a deep velvet laugh, and a reputation for rarely keeping a promise. In her tight tweed pants and long-tailed blazers and oversized ties, she moved effortlessly through the sea of gloves and lace and whispering society ladies.

When her wealthy family of Austrian royal lineage had found her erotic poetry embarrassing, Blanche had emancipated herself under the male nom de plume, which soon became a stage name as she strode into the theater world as playwright and actress, and eventually swelled into a total persona — the name with which she signed her letters, the name by which her intimates addressed her, the name of her self-image.

In her youth, Blanche had been named the most beautiful woman in Paris. Now, about to turn fifty-eight, Michael Strange was a ghost on a New York stage, her skin sallow, her body emaciated to the size of a child’s after refusing to let her aggressive leukemia keep her from performing.

Margaret and Michael had met seven years earlier. One day on Vinalhaven — the Maine island where Margaret would spend much of her life and write most of her books — she had rowed to a lover’s cottage and found the luscious stranger sunbathing there with her lover. Soon, back in New York, she was surprised to receive a lunch invitation from Michael, who had shown up dressed in fur from head to toe, asking bold questions about her love life while sipping sherry. Margaret was thirty, Michael fifty and on her third unhappy marriage; her latest husband had never read her poetry. Both women were born in the wrong century, bent on bending it to their will; both were accidental radicals, just by living unselfconsciously; both had had affairs with Thomas Wolfe; both were at heart poets more than anything else.

By the middle of the World War, they were lovers; Michael had declared that she had never loved anyone the way she loved Margaret and never would; she had promised to love her until her dying day.

Late one night, Margaret’s phone rang. Michael’s voice poured in, sped up with alarm, imploring her to get into a taxi right away. Her husband had found out about their relationship and, in an era when the diagnostic manual of psychiatry classified same-sex love as a mental illness, was threatening to have her locked away in an asylum. A doctor was on his way to “diagnose” her. With her maid’s help, Michael managed to slip out through the back staircase and into the taxi as Margaret was pulling up.

On the disorienting ride through the New York nocturne, they weighed their options and decided to head to the high-society women’s club Michael frequented. There, she collected herself, phoned her husband to demand a formal apology, then set the wheels in motion for a legal separation.

From this point on, Michael became — to use the modern term, hard-won and ahistorical — Margaret’s partner. Soon, they were living across the hallway from each other, in a pair of twin apartments on the East End, with Margaret part nominal tenant and part unnamed wife as she was quickly becoming one of the country’s most original and beloved children’s book authors.

It was a stormy love that pushed and pulled, but grafted itself onto Margaret’s being. Michael wrote adoring letters and criticized Margaret’s diction at dinner parties. She gave her a golden wishbone necklace and a ring, made her feel like she was too needy, and derided her children’s books as unsophisticated, “silly furry stories,” not Real Literature: an actress and socialite who had not published a poem in a decade and was feeling abandoned by her own muse, deriding one of the most vibrantly creative people of the past century — poet, songwriter, progressive education reformer, author of more than a hundred singularly wondrous books for the young, with which she would earn herself a little red house, a yellow convertible, and the love of millions of children; the author whom the visionary Ursula Nordstrom had no qualms calling her favorite author, despite also publishing Maurice Sendak, Shel Silverstein, and E.B. White. Even Michael’s pet name for Margaret was laced with this ambivalent mixture of affection and disdain: Bunny-no-good.

And yet nobody ever knows what electrifies the infinite sky between two people, what magnetizes them together, what roils deep beneath the faint surface trails left in letters and diaries and the recollections of bystanders, what animates the long days between the islanded moments crashed by emotion and frozen in time. Margaret loved Michael with unassailable devotion, and Michael was dying. So she did the hardest thing in life — facing the death of a beloved while remaining a pillar for their passage — the best way she knew how: She wrote a love letter in the form of a children’s book.

On the last day of spring in 1950, three years after Goodnight Moon had enraptured the world with its bright playfulness, The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds, somber and numinous with its elegiac prose, and its haunting duotone of otherworldly greens and yellows, and its simple dedication: “For Michael Strange.”…
