Why it is here: Engaging discussion on creativity and psychological suffering

The Pain in You and the God in You: Carl Jung on the Relationship Between Psychological Suffering and Creativity

By Maria Popova

When AI first began colonizing language — which is still our best instrument for bridging the abyss between us, a container for thought and feeling that shapes the contents — I asked chatGPT to compose a poem about a solar eclipse in the style of Walt Whitman. It returned a ledger of cliches in rhymed couplets. Getting the form wrong — Whitman did not rhyme — seemed like an easy correction by a line of code. Getting poetry itself wrong was the interesting question, the question that gets at the heart of why we make poems (or paintings or novels or songs) — a question fundamentally about what it means to be human.

I asked an elder poet friend why she thought chatGPT rang hollow where Whitman could compact infinities of feeling in a single image, could unseat the soul in a word.

She paused, then said: “Because AI hasn’t suffered.”

On the one hand, this echoes a dangerous myth: the archetype of the tortured genius handed down to us by the Romantics, who, cornered in their time and place, in a century of bloody revolutions, deadly epidemics, and punitive Puritanical norms, must have needed to believe that their suffering — those lives of poverty and privation, those ill-fated exercises in projection mistaken for love, all those premature deaths — was a fair price to pay for such creative volcanicity.

On the other hand, this is reality: Art is the music we make from the bewildered cry of being alive — sometimes a cry of exultant astonishment, but often a cry of devastation at the collision between our wishes and the will of the world. Every artist’s art is their coping mechanism for what they are living through — the longings, the heartbreaks, the triumphs, the wars within and without. It is these painful convolutions of the psyche — which used to be termed neurosis at the dawn of modern psychotherapy, and which we may simply call suffering — that reveal us to ourselves, and it is out of these revelations that we create anything capable of touching other lives, that contact we call art.

Our power and our freedom lie in learning to neither negate our suffering nor romanticize it but to harness its catalytic power as a current passing through us to jolt us alive, then passing on and down into the ground of being.

No one has refuted the myth of the tortured genius without negating the fact and fertility of suffering more pointedly than Carl Jung (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who thought deeply about the nature of creativity.

In 1943, a scholar of Kierkegaard asked Jung’s opinion of the relationship between “psychological problems” and creative genius. With an eye to Kierkegaard’s gift for letting his anxiety fuel rather than hinder his creativity, Jung declares him a “whole” person and not “a jangling hither and dither of displeasing fragmentary souls,” and writes:

True creative genius does not let itself be spoilt by analysis, but is freed from the impediments and distortions of a neurosis. Neurosis does not produce art. It is uncreative and inimical to life. It is failure and bungling. But the moderns mistake morbidity for creative birth — part of the general lunacy of our time.

It is, of course, an unanswerable question what an artist would have created if he had not been neurotic. Nietzsche’s syphilitic infection undoubtedly exerted a strongly neuroticizing influence on his life. But one could imagine a sound Nietzsche possessed of creative power without hypertension — something like Goethe. He would have written much the same as he did, but less strident, less shrill — i.e., less German — more restrained, more responsible, more reasonable and reverent.

A century before Alain de Botton offered his assuring perspective on the importance of breakdowns, Jung weighs what makes suffering generative or degenerative:

Neurosis is a justified doubt in oneself and continually poses the ultimate question of trust in man and in God. Doubt is creative if it is answered by deeds, and so is neurosis if it exonerates itself as having been a phase — a crisis which is pathological only when chronic. Neurosis is a protracted crisis degenerated into a habit, the daily catastrophe ready for use.

Jung considers the advice he would have given Kierkegaard about how to orient to his suffering, which was the raw material of his philosophical writings:

It doesn’t matter what you say, but what it says in you. To it you must address your answers. God is straightaway with you and is the voice within you. You have to have it out with that voice.

Couple with a forgotten young poet’s extraordinary letter to Emily Dickinson about how to bear your suffering, then revisit Kierkegaard himself on the value of despair.

Why it is here: Insightful piece on the importance of work in a meaningful life

Nobel-Winning Biochemist Gerty Cori on the Single Most Important Element of a Meaningful Life

We call it “the long run,” life, and spend it trying to understand what keeps us running, trying to run toward, to see the true goal through all the false trophies promised us by the merchants of approval and acclaim.

What keeps the body running is glycogen — the essential fuel of muscles. What keeps the soul running is a substance we must each synthesize out of the mystery we are. There are two kinds of running the soul does: running away from — our fears, our past, our mistakes — and running toward. The first kind is easier, for it is reflexive. The second kind is life’s most difficult, most rewarding work — to discover the track on which to run and its most authentic destination, to synthesize out of our dreams and desires the glycogen of a strong animating spirit to fuel the long run of a purposeful, substantive, meaningful life.

Czech biochemist Gerty Cori (August 15, 1896–October 26, 1957) — the third woman to win the Nobel Prize in science, for her discovery of how glycogen works in the body — articulated with poetic precision the animating spirit of a purposeful life when she appeared on Edward R. Murrow’s popular radio series This I Believe in the late summer of 1952:

The love for and dedication to one’s work seems to me the basis for happiness… For a [scientist], the unforgotten moments of life are those rare ones, which come after years of plodding work, when the veil over nature’s secret seems suddenly to lift and when what was dark and chaotic appears in a clear and beautiful light and pattern.

This clarity of vision is not singular to science. Pulsating beneath Cori’s words is the insistence that a meaningful life — one that makes the long run worthy of running — springs from devotion to work, any work, that parts the veil of meaninglessness to reveal a glimpse of some greater truth. The most alive people I know, whether they make postulates or poems, furniture or film, are animated by such devotion. It is the best antidote to the existential catatonia of cynicism and despair that leaves people too petrified to live up to and into their gifts. Cori observes:

I believe that art and science are the glories of the human mind… Contemplation of the great human achievements through the ages is helpful to me in moments of despair and doubt. Human folly then seems less important… I believe that cynicism and despair and the straitjacket into which totalitarian systems try to force the human mind are inimical to first rate achievements in art and science.

Why it is here: In-depth exploration of a historical legal case with cultural significance, providing a rich context for learning about literature and legal history.

The lawsuit at the center of Charles Dickensâs Bleak House, which ran in monthly installments from 1852 to 1853, is a family dispute over a will that has been in the Court of Chancery for so long that âno man alive knows what it means.â When Jarndyce and Jarndyce is finally wound up, the estate it was fought over is gone: it has been âabsorbed in costs,â as the novel puts it. So which real case was Dickens poking at?

The answer youâll hear most often comes with a doozy of a number attached, a suit filed in 1798 that supposedly dragged on until 1915.

Two Suits, No Names

Dickens kicked off the guessing game himself in the preface he wrote in August 1853, the same one where he defended the spontaneous combustion of Krook: he insisted that âeverything set forth in these pages concerning the Court of Chancery is substantially true, and within the truth,â and then pointed to two real cases without naming either one. The first had been going for nearly 20 years and had cost Â£70,000, and was, he wrote, âA FRIENDLY SUIT.â The second, still undecided, âwas commenced before the close of the last century and in which more than double the amount of seventy thousand pounds has been swallowed up in costs.â

The first is usually identified as the fight over the will of Charles Day, a rich manufacturer of boot blacking, which is a nice irony for a man who spent part of his childhood pasting labels on blacking pots. The second, according to legal historian Patrick Polden, was the Jennens case.

William the Rich

William Jennens died at his country house in Acton, Suffolk, in June 1798, in his late 90s. The Monthly Magazine called him the supposed richest commoner in England. The Gentlemanâs Magazine said his property was thought to be worth at least Â£2 million, that dividends on most of his stocks hadnât been collected since 1788, and that an iron chest held Â£19,000 in banknotes from that year. It also reported a will found in his coat pocket, sealed but never signed: according to his favorite servant, Jennens had left his spectacles at home on the day he went to his lawyer to sign it, and then forgot about it.

So the estate went to his relatives under the law, and for more than a century people named Jennens or Jennings, in Britain and in the U.S., tried to prove they were the ones who should have gotten it. In January 1915, American papers ran an Associated Press item about the death of David Jennings in the Wolverhampton workhouse, âfamous in legal circlesâ as a claimant to the âJenningsâ Millions,â which the item said Dickens had used as the basis for Jarndyce and Jarndyce. That may be where the 1915 end date comes from, though one version of the story noted that the case hadnât been reopened in about 40 years.

The Case Against the Case

The 117-year version says the case ended when legal fees had eaten the whole estate, just like in the book. Polden, who went through the court records for a two-part study in the Common Law World Review, says that isnât what happened. Jennensâs property was handed out to his next of kin, and the lawsuits that followed were separate claims by would-be heirs, who lost every significant ruling but one. In Jennens, he writes, âthere was no such fund, no ongoing case and the deadly refrain of âcosts in the causeâ did not echo down the years.â The litigation had been dormant for 15 years by the time Dickens started writing Bleak House in November 1851, and Polden calls the idea that Dickens fictionalized it âseriously misleading.â

Polden does allow that Dickens may have been thrown by a strange news episode in 1852, when papers announced the case had been settled and then took it back. And there were other candidates all along. The will of Peter Thellusson, who died in 1797, was fought over in court until the House of Lords upheld it in 1806, and a new dispute over the fortune broke out in 1858. The only link Polden found that really ties the Jennens case to the novel is a backward one: once Bleak House started coming out, people said the real case resembled the fictional one.

Ripper, the unhinged officer one button-press away from ordering an unwarranted nuclear strike. Not for the faint of heart, this eerie crime drama, based on the book by Anthony Burgess, follows young hoodlum and his cold-hearted gang of âdroogs'âas they rampage through a truly disturbing version of England. Malcolm McDowellâs portrayal of Alex is a thing of wonder.

8. Lolita (1962) // 83%

As controversial as it is misunderstood, Kubrick adapted Vladimir Nabokovâs story of an older man's obsession with an underage girl with insight and bravery. William Makepeace Thackeray's classic novel about an 18th century Irishman's ruthless climb to the heights of English nobility is transformed by Kubrick into a optically sumptuous affair, with Ryan O'Neal a commanding presence as Lyndon.

Kubrick's sole foray into the horror genre was truly groundbreaking. Based on the novel by Stephen King, The Shining stands as one of the best of its kind, with Jack Nicholson starring as a struggling writer who makes the unwise decision to take a job as caretaker of an isolated hotel.

Brentford aim for 'special things' after ending 89-year Old Trafford wait

"Slightly surreal."

That is how Brentford manager Keith Andrews summed up the club's first win at Manchester United in 89 years.

The Bees may have been waiting nearly nine decades to win at Old Trafford, but ended that run in style by thrashing Mauricio Pochettino's strugglers 4-0 on Saturday.

Brentford's last win at United before this weekend was in February 1937 - the longest any side has gone between victories against the Red Devils, surpassing Bristol City's 69-year wait between 1909 and 1978.

Granted, Brentford had only played eight games on United's turf since then, given the clubs' contrasting fortunes.

But the emphatic way in which they ended that streak is surely cause for celebration for a club who just 12 years ago were competing in League One.

"Slightly surreal if I am honest," Brentford boss Andrews told BBC Match of the Day.

"We have been keen to enjoy the journey. We want to be really ambitious but [with a] level of humility. I think we can achieve special things because I think it is a special group."

Brentford have cemented their status as an established Premier League club but "special things" suggests Andrews sees his side going even further.

After a second consecutive 4-0 win, having thrashed Everton by the same score on Monday, the Bees are now fifth in the league and with European football in their sights.

Andrews surpassing expectation

Andrews' appointment at Brentford in 2025 divided opinion after the departure of Thomas Frank, who had rightly earned the adoration of the fans having led them to the top flight.

While some fans trusted the judgement of the board, others suggested hiring someone who had never been a first-team manager before showed a lack of ambition.

There can now be little debate around Andrews' position.

The Irishman was handed a new contract in February - just eight months into the job - and after finishing 10th last season, he has his sights set on more this campaign.

"I haven't been doing this for very long, but it has been a special week," the 46-year-old told Sky Sports after the win at Old Trafford.

"I thought we were well worthy of getting the three points. We could have been more clinical and that was the message at half-time.

"Could we take the handbrake off more? Could we go for it? I fancy us all the time when we're in those areas.

"Twelve games in and we're in a good groove. We feel we do a lot of things right."

The former midfielder's strategy to go for more rather than defend their 2-0 half-time lead speaks volumes for how he views the potential in his side - and it ultimately paid off as they further punished United's frailties.

When asked about making history at United, Andrews referenced legendary Bees boss Harry Curtis - Brentford's longest-serving and most successful manager to date.

"First one in the Premier League and first win since Harry Curtis was manager," he said.

"They were special days for Brentford going back a long time. Now it is nice to be part of the current journey."

Bees set sights on Europe

Since promotion to the top flight in 2021, the closest Brentford have come to relegation was when they finished 16th under Frank in 2023-24.

They have taken to life in the Premier League with relative ease - a remarkable achievement given they were competing in League Two less than 20 years ago.

Forward Callum Wilson who scored his first top-flight goals for Brentford with a double against United - in the absence of injured striker Igor Thiago - said the club are aiming high.

"It is a smaller club that does everything to the maximum of their abilities," he said.

"Everyone on the inside feels they belong at this level. The club's next step in their transition is to win a trophy or step up to Europe.

"Back-to-back 4-0s, which is nice, but it comes down to the hard work that everyone puts in behind the scenes.

"It was a nice moment and everyone got to celebrate at the end."

Following victory over the Toffees last week Andrews called for critics of his side to "get real", suggesting expectation levels had spiralled considering their journey.

"The expectation levels, I think, at this club have changed and maybe the outside world have changed a little bit," he said.

"Regardless of the performance or the result... there's still a little bit swirling in the air - we're a little bit unhappy or should they be doing a little bit better?

"Maybe people need to get a little bit real.

"I'm really happy with our group. I'm really happy with our football club and long may that continue."

New Zealand bounced back from their record 25-point defeat to England to stun Steve Borthwick's charges a week on with a 26-8 Nations Championship victory at Allianz Stadium Twickenham.

England actually scored the opening points via a long-range Henry Slade penalty in the third minute, but did not trouble the scoreboard again in torrential Twickenham rain until the 75th minute - hooker Jamie George scoring a maul try.

The All Blacks scored tries in either half through No 8 Wallace Sititi and scrum-half Cam Roigard - the latter a stunning finish in the corner - as Dave Rennie's side produced a thorough dismantling of the hosts.

Fly-half Richie Mo'unga also kicked superbly for the visitors, landing both conversions and four penalties against an ill-disciplined England, who were shown yellow cards to lock Alex Coles (high tackle) and replacement back-row Henry Pollock (offside, repeat team penalties).

New Zealand lock Scott Barrett was also shown yellow late on for repeat team penalties, but by then the All Blacks were home and hosed as far as the result was concerned against a shocked England.

As if to sum up England's miserable day, Marcus Smith near comically ended up on his backside while attempting the straightforward conversion for George's late try, leaving England stuck in single digits for points for the first time in over three years (August 2023).

Story of the match

Less than a minute into the contest, New Zealand's starting scrum-half Cortez Ratima was penalised for failing to release in a jackal attempt on halfway, with England's Slade stepping up to notch three points off the tee from distance.

Two big chances then came and went for the hosts. First, a maul collapse handed England a lineout deep in the 22, only for Anton Segner to rise and steal it, before Coles then spilled the ball on the run within the 22 as a try looked likely.

The All Blacks made England pay for such profligacy, with Rieko Ioane and Ratima breaks paving the way for Sititi to finish strongly from close range in the 17th minute.

Mo'unga converted for the full haul, with England then suffering two further pointless visits to the New Zealand 22 - the second particularly costly as Slade kicked dead with a penalty kick from hand.

England were then reduced to 14 six minutes from half-time with Coles sin-binned for a head-on-head tackle on opposite number Fabian Holland.

Despite missing out via a five-metre lineout maul, New Zealand would stretch their lead to seven before the break, as Mo'unga struck over after Tommy Freeman had cheaply kicked the ball away to deny the visitors the chance to take a Roigard 50:22 quickly.

The second half started poorly for England from the off as they knocked on the restart, and though Freddie Steward produced a crunching tackle on Damian McKenzie, a breakdown penalty saw Mo'unga stretch the lead to 10 points.

Could MSC Cruises soon be as big with North Americans as it is with Europeans?

That's the goal at the fast-growing Europe-based line, which is in the midst of a major expansion into the North American market.

In an exclusive interview this week aboard the line's newest ship, MSC World Asia, MSC Cruises CEO Gianni Onorato told TPG the brand is aiming for 5 million American passengers a year within a decade — more than double the number it carries now.

It'll get there in part by growing its North American passenger count to 50% of its business, up from around 30% to 35% today, he said — a shift in passenger mix that would make North Americans the biggest segment of its customers.

"The cruise industry has always been, is today, and will be tomorrow represented by 50% North American guests, and I believe that MSC should reflect this share," Onorato said during a one-on-one interview on MSC World Asia as it was being unveiled in France.

The debut of MSC World Asia — at 216,638 gross tons, one of the largest cruise vessels ever built — ties into MSC Cruises' growth strategy for North American customers as it'll sail in North America starting late next year after initial sailings in the Mediterranean.

It'll operate a series of seven- and 14-night winter sailings in the Southern Caribbean out of Martinique, Guadeloupe and Barbados that'll complement the line's growing number of Caribbean itineraries out of Florida and Galveston, Texas.

It's just the latest big new ship that MSC Cruises has earmarked for North America as part of its North American growth strategy.

The line's 19-month-old MSC World America, a sister ship to MSC World Asia that also is among the biggest cruise vessels ever built, already is sailing out of Florida.

Custom-built for the North American market in a way no other MSC Cruises ship has been before, MSC World America is significantly bigger and more venue-packed than any other ship MSC Cruises has deployed to the region.

A third ship in the same series debuting in late 2027, MSC World Atlantic, also will be devoted to the North American market with sailings out of Port Canaveral, Florida.

All three of the ships are part of the line's new World Class series, which are by far the biggest MSC Cruises vessels ever built. Capable of carrying nearly 6,800 passengers with every berth filled, they are the first to rival the biggest ships from cruise giant Royal Caribbean in size and amenities.

In all, MSC Cruises will have seven vessels sailing out of U.S. ports for all or part of 2027, plus another two vessels sailing from Caribbean ports, for a total of nine ships in North America. That's an enormous increase from just a few years ago. As recently as 2017, MSC Cruises had just one ship sailing year-round from a U.S. port plus a handful more sailing from Caribbean ports.

With the addition of MSC World Asia, MSC Cruises has 24 vessels in all.

The expanded footprint in North America includes MSC Cruises' first sailings to Alaska, which began in May, and its first sailings from Galveston, which began in December.

MSC Cruises also has invested heavily the past few years in North American port infrastructure and a private destination in the region, the Ocean Cay MSC Marine Reserve in the Bahamas.

Onorato told TPG the line eventually could expand its North American cruise offerings to more U.S. ports, though not for a few years.

"This is an opportunity with us, and we will be looking at this," he said. "But not in the very short term. We're not [planning this] for 27, for 28 or for 29 yet. But in the future, why not?"

Onorato noted the line needs to balance its growth in North America with its growth in Europe, where it wants to maintain its dominant position.

"We don't want to reduce the capacity in Europe, because in Europe today we are living a situation of market leadership, which I like a lot, and so I don't want to lose it," he said.

Onorato also noted the company is growing significantly in Asia with an announcement earlier this month that it would deploy a second ship to the region starting in late 2028. It'll offer cruises out of Singapore.

Staying strong in Europe, in particular, ties into the company's strategy to grow North American passenger counts as Americans can become a bigger feeder market into the brand's Europe-based ships, Onorato suggested.

"I believe being the leader in Europe ... we are the ideal cruise line for North Americans traveling to Europe, because we have so many different embarkation ports," he said.

Onorato noted that MSC Cruises lets passengers board its ships in 10 different ports around the Mediterranean, far more than any of the North American brands operating in the region, with departures starting every day of the week.

These include departures from such secondary ports as Marseille, France; Genoa, Italy; and Naples, Italy. The latter, he noted, can now be reached via daily nonstop United and Delta flights from the United States.

MSC Cruises has five more of its new World Class ships on order for delivery by 2031. It also has ordered a new class of four slightly smaller vessels to debut between 2030 and 2033.

Toegether, the nine ships will increase the line's capacity by nearly 50%.

Inside Fresno Unified’s Prop. 28-Funded Push for Sustainable Arts Education

The district's $13 million budget largely expanded elementary school arts instruction.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

David Hunter, known for sporting colorful ties printed with art palettes and paintbrushes, is popular among his elementary students. Not only for his eccentric fashion sense, but also because, for many young children in Fresno Unified School District, he is their introduction to the arts.

“Every kid knows who I am and what I’m there to do, and that gives them a lot of joy,” Hunter, a former traditional classroom teacher, said. “They all enjoy having art, and I’m actually there tying it into what they’re learning.”

California’s third-largest school district has dramatically expanded arts education over the past three years, largely due to Proposition 28. The 2022 voter-approved measure sets aside roughly $1 billion annually for California schools to expand the arts for TK-12 students.

But that windfall has brought new challenges for California schools. For decades, arts programs were the first to go with budget cuts. Now, school leaders must quickly spend millions in annual arts funds while navigating a shortage of credentialed arts educators, confusion around spending rules and new standards for art, music, dance and theater programs.

California schools spent about 96% of their Prop. 28 funds from the 2023-2024 school year, the first year of Prop. 28’s rollout, according to the California Department of Education. About 340 school districts, charter schools and county offices of education that did not spend all of their funds will lose a total of $32.9 million in arts education funding next year.

Fresno Unified, with the state’s third-largest allocation of Prop. 28 funds, spent all of its $13 million allocation for the first year. The district hired itinerant instructors to serve all school sites and focused on expanding arts education for elementary schools.

Heather Kuyper-McKeithen, arts education manager for Fresno Unified, said the district zeroed in on two elementary school programs: arts integration (which incorporates the arts into core academic instruction) and dance. Elementary schools must choose to participate in one or the other.

Kuyper-McKeithen said Fresno Unified was able to build its arts programs because it recruited arts teachers early in the rollout of Prop. 28 and educators were “willing to paint the bus while it is going down the road.”

“Everyone was also so used to grant money disappearing after a few years, that we had to think more strategically with an eye towards the long term,” Kuyper-McKeithen told EdSource in October.

Since 2023, Fresno Unified has hired 56 new full-time equivalent arts educators, including 25 full-time dance teachers and 20 elementary arts integration teachers for its 72 elementary schools.

Like a lot of other districts, Fresno Unified has struggled to find enough credentialed arts educators. The district expanded its dance and arts integration programs largely by transferring existing staff into arts teaching roles as they worked to earn new credentials.

Most arts integration teachers, for example, previously taught as traditional classroom teachers and already have multiple-subject teaching credentials. They must earn their supplemental arts credential, or pass the California Subject Examinations for Teachers, within three years on the new assignment.

Many dance instructors also taught under physical education credentials, and can earn their dance credential — which can take up to two years — while teaching in their Prop. 28-funded roles.

Hunter, the arts integration teacher and coordinator at Fresno Unified, helped launch and grow the arts integration program from eight teachers serving 16 schools to 20 teachers serving 40 schools since 2023. Arts integration has gained traction in recent years as a teaching model that may improve learning in core subjects, strengthen retention and support cognitive and social-emotional development by weaving arts into academics.

Hunter previously worked as a classroom teacher and now teaches arts integration lessons in seven elementary classrooms a day between Thomas Elementary and Holland Elementary.

Shock! A prime minister wants to get noticed by voters who are not obsessed with politics. The resident of No 10 cares about their image.

Except, hang on, neither of these things are remotely surprising. Margaret Thatcher used to phone in to chat to the Radio 2 DJ Jimmy Young - millions listening at home, doing the washing up, or with the chat humming in the background at work.

Winston Churchill didn't just like smoking big fat cigars, he posed deliberately with them - scowling in one of his most famous pictures, because the photographer had plucked the stogie out of his aristocratic mouth.

While Westminster has got itself in a spin over Andy Burnham's social media habits this week, the questions are not, should he care about who he is communicating with, or try to cultivate a certain image? The answers to both questions are no brainer yeses. The dilemma is whether Downing Street's efforts have gone too far?

The whole fuss stemmed from a video posted by an online influencer who'd been at a Downing Street shindig. No 10 says the post by Max Balegde, a TV presenter and social media personality whose real name is Max Trobe, was unacceptable, and he's deleted it.

The PM's rivals attacked him for what happened. And it's sent parts of the press into a froth, with accusations that Burnham dodges scrutiny and tough, traditional questioning, preferring to DJ and hope that influencers' youthful cool rubs off on him.

From the first black T-shirt-wearing Instagram post when he started his by-election campaign (the second video was him unboxing campaign leaflets with an Oasis soundtrack, natch), it was obvious Burnham would try to play a strong social media game.

And since he's moved into No 10, he's devoted more time and political energy than any of his predecessors to social media platforms like Tiktok or Instagram, websites like Ladbible or popular podcasts like How to Fail.

Whatever you watch, read or listen to, and by reading this article you too are using a form of non traditional media because you are reading online, there is no point clutching your pearls about the prime minister and his team using everything available to try to reach voters.

"The comments outside No 10 were undeniably offensive and the whole thing is unedifying," one senior Westminster journalist told me. "But does it matter in the grand scheme of things? This isn't new - successive prime ministers have attempted to go direct to influencers with mixed success for many years now."

Before influencers there were plenty of attempts, some cringeworthy, some meaningful, by prime ministers to extend their influence beyond speaking in Parliament, to the established print press, or the main broadcasters.

Tony Blair popped up on Richard and Judy's sofa, although he might rather forget when he got dragged into the quiz, "You Say We Pay" and didn't do very well. David Cameron took questions from Gemma Collins and Joey Essex for Heat magazine, declining being featured in "Torso of the Week".

I'm reliably told one future prime minister's team asked someone doing work experience to suggest pop songs young people were listening to before going on the radio to discuss their favourite music so he'd look down with the kids.

Separately, Gordon Brown once claimed to be an Arctic Monkeys fan, although later couldn't name any of their songs, and could only say, "They are very loud". In time, he admitted it had all been a PR disaster.

What's different about Burnham is the scale of his 2020s-friendly comms. Arguably, that's a reflection of the sprawl of the modern media.

Perhaps some of the kickback has been because parts of the media fear their influence is being drowned out by the noise from a busier and busier online landscape. Although it's also worth saying many traditional outlets, including the BBC, also have huge presences on their own digital platforms and social media, with more podcasts, posts, and pieces than you could ever dream of.

No 10 might crack a smile of irony seeing established media voices thundering online about activity online. Despite this week's embarrassment, they have no intention of shifting their strategy.

Acknowledging it sounded almost too good to be true, one insider told me on a hospital visit in Watford at the start of the month, a member of the public passing the PM in the corridor grabbed his arm and said, "I follow you on TikTok, you give us hope".

But the row this week highlights what is a simple truth â all content is not created equally â there are important differences in who, and how.

When it comes to influencers, Burnham's team may now think more carefully about exactly who they invite through the door.

One experienced Westminster editor said: "Clearly Burnham's team didn't vet the influencers enough - no-one wants a row about offensive material ending up being the story, when really you were just trying to be a bit cool and appeal to the kids."

A prominent content creator told me: "I think it's a great idea for No 10 to involve content creators in their comms strategy, I'm somewhat suspicious of the types of influencers on Burnham's list. There are plenty of journalistic content creators with large followings and engaged audiences who seem to be missing. Is it because they will be more inclined to hold him to account, perhaps?"

Influencers and content creators don't do the same job as journalists, and aren't pretending to either. They might agree to conditions journalists would not accept - sometimes they're not allowed to film footage themselves, and one told me they had to submit questions to a minister before an interview.

One senior political journalist told me: "The problem is when access starts being prioritised for people whose job is to make content, rather than ask questions. If influencers get the access without the scrutiny, it's the public who lose out."…

Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it

For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.

The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.

The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.

"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.

Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.

But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.

Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.

In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.

The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.

If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.

"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."

Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.

One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.

Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.

"Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.

But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.…
